items.title: MSF South Sudan: Abduction of staff members forces MSF to suspend all activities in Yei River County

original_payload.original_title: MSF South Sudan: Abduction of staff members forces MSF to suspend all activities in Yei River County
original_payload.original_body:
South Sudan
MSF South Sudan: Abduction of staff members forces MSF to suspend all activities in Yei River County
Format
News and Press Release
Source
MSF
Posted
23 Nov 2026
Originally published
23 Nov 2026
Juba, 23 November 2026  — Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders (MSF) suspended all its activities for a minimum of three months starting Tuesday 17 November, in South Sudan’s Yei River County, Central Equatoria State, after armed assailants abducted an MSF staff member and a Ministry of Health midwife on Thursday 12 November. Although both staff members were released unharmed on Saturday 14 November, this incident highlights the continuation of violence against healthcare workers in South Sudan. ​
MSF denounces in the strongest terms the abduction of humanitarian and medical workers as utterly unacceptable. MSF calls upon authorities and other actors to take responsibility and act decisively to put an end to these incidents. ​
"The suspension of services was a painful and uneasy decision, given the people's needs in the area, particularly among vulnerable groups, such as pregnant and lactating women, children and the elderly," says Dr Ferdinand Atte, MSF's Head of Mission in South Sudan. "In addition, we had to suspend MSF’s support to the Ebola preparedness, in particular for the management of the isolation facility, which could have dramatic consequences in case of the outbreak in the area."
Only a substantial, sustained and verifiable improvement in the security environment, together with concrete measures to prevent and actively combat abduction crimes would allow MSF to restart activities. At present, no such conditions are in place. "MSF cannot continue operating in Yei area while abductions are now taking place even within the town. The safety and security of our staff comes first," adds Dr Atte.
In August 2025, MSF was forced to temporarily suspend all activities in the same county following two abductions in just over a week. "Following last year's abductions, we received verbal assurances from authorities that medical staff and patients would be safe and protected within the 5-mile radius around Yei," adds Dr Atte. However, on 17 November, armed assailants stopped the MSF ambulance approximately 3 miles from the town.
The MSF driver and Ministry of Health midwife were abducted after an MSF ambulance was stopped at gunpoint by unknown armed assailants while heading back to Jansuk from the Yei Civil Hospital, after referring patients. The incident took place 500 metres from the Jansuk primary healthcare facility.
This was the fifth abduction affecting MSF in Yei River County since 2024, following a period of bombardments, attacks, looting and vandalism of MSF facilities throughout South Sudan. All actors must fulfil their obligations to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, including healthcare workers, patients, and medical facilities. Healthcare workers must never be targeted. ​
MSF was supporting Yei Civil Hospital and Jansuk clinic, performing community-based care for gender-based violence, as well as establishing the Ebola Isolation Unit with 10-beds capacity, the only such facility in the County.
Note to Editors:
MSF provides medical care to people affected by conflict, displacement and disease outbreaks across six states and two administrative areas in South Sudan, including in areas where hospitals are difficult to reach. MSF has been present in what is today South Sudan since 1983 and remains one of the largest medical humanitarian agencies in the country. From January to October 2026, MSF provided more than 719,349 outpatient consultations (including for children under 5), inpatient care for over 99,658 patients (including 8,771 surgeries), and screened 303,063 children for malnutrition.

items.title: DR Congo's Bakole to fight Wilder on Fury-Joshua undercard

original_payload.original_title: DR Congo's Bakole to fight Wilder on Fury-Joshua undercard
original_payload.original_body:
Wilder to fight Bakole on Fury-Joshua undercard
Image source,  Getty Images
Image caption,    Former world champion Deontay Wilder (left) has 45 wins, four defeats and one draw, while Martin Bakole has 21 wins, two defeats and one draw
By  Kal Sajad   BBC Sport boxing journalist
Published
7 hours ago
Heavyweight Martin Bakole will face former world champion Deontay Wilder on the undercard of Tyson Fury's fight with Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December.
The 33-year-old Congolese fighter replaces Australian Jai Opetaia, who  withdrew after aggravating a hand injury in training.
Scotland-based Bakole had been scheduled to fight unbeaten Nigerian Solomon Adebayo on the bill, but will instead face 41-year-old Wilder in the co-main event.
Bakole suffered a second-round knockout defeat by Joseph Parker in  February 2025 , having accepted the fight on just two days' notice.
He then fought to a majority draw with Nigerian Efe Ajagba in May 2025 and has not competed since.
Former WBC heavyweight champion Wilder, who has 43 knockouts in 45 victories, is looking to build on his split-decision win over Britain's Derek Chisora in  April .
Unbeaten cruiserweight Opetaia, 31, was set to make his heavyweight debut against Wilder but pulled out of the contest last week.
Several British heavyweights, including Chisora, Richard Riakporhe, Frazer Clarke and Johnny Fisher had expressed an interest in facing Wilder following Opetaia's withdrawal.
Fury v Joshua - boxing's epic unfinished story
Who else is on the Fury-Joshua undercard?
Fury and Joshua's long-awaited showdown has been more than a decade in the making.
After years of failed negotiations, the fight was finally agreed with the financial backing of Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh and will be streamed globally on Netflix.
They are expected to contest the WBA 'super' heavyweight title at Cardiff's Principality Stadium, with ringwalks planned for no earlier than 01:00 GMT on Saturday, 12 December.
But despite the magnitude of the main event, the undercard has so far failed to match the anticipation surrounding one of the biggest fights in British boxing history.
Wilder remains a recognisable name among British fans, largely because of his memorable trilogy with Fury, but a contest against Bakole is unlikely to capture the imagination of the wider public.
Boxing records website BoxRec currently lists only Fury-Joshua on the event, although Netflix has announced further bouts in a social media post.
Welsh heavyweight  Moses Jolly  (12-0-1, 8 KOs) will face Brazil's  Igor Macedo , who has won 15 of his 16 professional fights, with 14 victories by knockout.
Swansea-fighter Jolly, 30, is unbeaten and last fought in August, when he drew with Italian Guido Vianello at London's O2 Arena.
Unbeaten 21-year-old American prospect  Da'Mazion Vanhouter  (14-0, 11 KOs) will face Belgium's  Michael Essomba  (11-2, 10 KOs) in another heavyweight contest.
Boxing great Manny Pacquiao and Cardiff's former world champion Joe Cordina had both been linked with appearances on the undercard, although Pacquiao is no longer expected to feature.
It remains unclear whether any further bouts will be added to the event.

items.title: Uganda: Booze Kills 17,000 in Uganda, Costs Country $3billion Per Year

original_payload.original_title: Uganda: Booze Kills 17,000 in Uganda, Costs Country $3billion Per Year
original_payload.original_body:
Kampala — Uganda is losing an estimated 17,000 people annually to alcohol-related harm, while the economic cost of excessive consumption is estimated at Shs11 trillion (about $2.95 billion) a year, according to research findings released Friday.
The findings presented by the Uganda Alcohol Policy Alliance (UAPA) at the Grand Global Hotel in Kampala, suggest that alcohol-related harm extends well beyond addiction, contributing to premature deaths, illness, road crashes, domestic violence, lost productivity and pressure on healthcare services.
The assessment, an 80-page synthesis of research compiled by specialists from Makerere University School of Public Health, Mbarara University of Science and Technology, the Uganda Cancer Institute and partner institutions, places Uganda among the world's highest alcohol-consuming countries.

items.title: Maroc: un «mode d'emploi» remis aux entreprises pour exporter en Chine sans droits de douane

original_payload.original_title: Maroc: un «mode d'emploi» remis aux entreprises pour exporter en Chine sans droits de douane
original_payload.original_body:
Maroc: un «mode d'emploi» remis aux entreprises pour exporter en Chine sans droits de douane
Au Maroc, le ministre chargé du Commerce extérieur, Omar Hejira, a remis, le week-end dernier, aux entreprises marocaines le « mode d'emploi » pour profiter du régime de droits de douanes à 0 % appliqué par la Chine sur les exportations africaines, une mesure officialisée au mois de mai dernier par Pékin.
Mettre RFI en favori sur Google
pour voir les contenus de RFI s’afficher en priorité dans vos résultats de recherche.
Publié le :  24/11/2026 - 01:12
1 min     Temps de lecture
Le port de Tanger Med, au nord du Maroc, le 10 juillet 2025.        AFP - ABDEL MAJID BZIOUAT
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Même si le royaume chérifien ne fait pas partie des partenaires économiques majeurs de la Chine sur le continent africain, les échanges entre les deux pays sont, certes, en nette progression ces dernières années, mais également très déséquilibrés.
«  Les exportateurs marocains sont invités à saisir cette opportunité pour adresser le marché chinois marqué par une demande importante et diversifiée  », peut-on lire dans une circulaire transmise aux entreprises marocaines par le ministre du Commerce extérieur.
Très peu de contraintes sont édictées pour être exemptées des droits de douane chinois, si ce n'est respecter ce taux de 40 %, soit la teneur minimale en valeur régionale – la TVR – qui correspond à la part de matières locales dans l'élaboration d'un produit.
«  C'est une opportunité importante  », estime Driss Effina, économiste marocain, avant d’ajouter qu’«  il y a quelques créneaux compétitifs pour le Maroc comme le phosphate et ses dérivés.  »
Pour autant,  « le Maroc n'y gagnera pas grand-chose, étant donné les produits que le pays peut exporter. Cela peut réduire un peu, mais ne comblera pas le déficit commercial colossal qui existe entre les deux pays  », précise l'économiste.
En effet, même si les échanges commerciaux entre Pékin et Rabat ont atteint, pour la première fois, 10 milliards de dollars en 2025, les importations chinoises restent encore très largement majoritaires, ayant aussi augmenté en 2025.
Selon Driss Effina, «  ces exonérations ne suffiront pas, il faudra des quotas d'importations  », indispensables pour équilibrer les échanges.

items.title: Tunisie: à Monastir, la pollution textile et les eaux usées détruisent la baie

original_payload.original_title: Tunisie: à Monastir, la pollution textile et les eaux usées détruisent la baie
original_payload.original_body:
Reportage Afrique
Tunisie: à Monastir, la pollution textile et les eaux usées détruisent la baie
Publié le :  24/11/2026 - 00:10
Écouter - 02:24
Depuis des années, les associations de défense environnementale dénoncent la pollution marine dans la baie de Monastir, une ville côtière de l’Est tunisien à 162 kilomètres de Tunis. En cause, les rejets de l’industrie textile et la saturation des trois stations d’épuration sur place qui empêchent un traitement correct des eaux usées. Le tout se déverse dans le golfe de Monastir, causant un «  crime environnemental  », selon les déclarations du président Kaïs Saïed, qui s’était rendu sur place en juillet 2025. Un an après, la situation a empiré, selon les pêcheurs et les ONG présents sur place.
Dans la baie de Monastir, le déversement des eaux usées et la pollution textile détruisent les écosystèmes. Photo prise à Ksibet el-Mediouni en novembre 2026, à 10 kilomètres de Monastir.        © Lilia Blaise / RFI
Publicité
De notre envoyée spéciale à Ksibet el-Mediouni,
À Ksibet el-Mediouni, près de Monastir, la mer est calme, mais malgré le beau temps, Mounir Hassine n'ira pas se baigner. Le président de la section locale du   Forum pour les droits économiques et sociaux     dénonce depuis des années l'impact de la pollution marine sur la baie. «  En général, la pollution existe toujours dans cette eau , explique-t-il,  parce qu'il y a des versements anarchiques, soit des   industries textiles  , soit des stations d'épuration. Par exemple, la station d'épuration de Sayada-Lamta-Bouhjar, c'est une petite station qui n'a pas d'émissaire : elle verse directement sur la plage. Et cette station a une capacité journalière qui ne dépasse pas 1 680 m³ par jour. Actuellement, elle reçoit plus de 9   000 mètres cubes par jour, donc elle est totalement débordée.  »
Les rejets des eaux usées et industrielles dans la mer provoquent une croissance d'algues, des «  salades vertes  » comme les surnomme Mounir. Ces algues asphyxient la vie marine ou provoquent le phénomène de mer rouge avec l'augmentation des températures en été. «  Juste après le phénomène de mer rouge , poursuit-il,  on assiste à une mort massive de toute la faune de la baie.  »
À lire aussi  Tunisie: à Gabès, des militants antipollution entre lassitude et volonté de ne pas abandonner leur ville
«  C'est simple, ici, tout est mort  »
Au port, les pêcheurs se font rares, car beaucoup n'arrivent plus à travailler, comme Sami Benchir, qui a trente ans d'expérience en mer. «  Écoutez, c'est simple, ici, tout est mort , déplore-t-il.  Moi, avant, si je ne pêchais pas, je me baignais ici, je voyais les poissons à l'œil nu. Là, il n'y a plus rien, donc on part pêcher ailleurs.  »
Plusieurs bateaux sont au sol, sur le quai, leurs coques abîmées par la pollution, forçant les pêcheurs à les nettoyer et repeindre fréquemment, selon Mounir. «  La couleur rouge brique devient grise, c'est la réaction chimique, le rythme des entretiens s'est accéléré  », observe-t-il.
Faouzi Ouanes, un autre pêcheur, estime qu'il existe des solutions. «  Moi, je parle souvent avec les gens de l'Office national de l'assainissement , raconte-t-il.  Ils me disent que, dans l'immédiat, c'est compliqué, mais je pense qu'on pourrait avoir des citernes ou des camions qui viennent au moins délester les stations lorsqu'elles sont saturées.  »
Face aux alertes récurrentes de la société civile, le gouvernement a prévu plusieurs plans de dépollution, dont l'aménagement de nouvelles stations d'épuration. Mais pour Mounir Hassine, le temps presse face à l'urgence écologique.
À lire aussi  L'inaction face à la pollution plastique pourrait coûter jusqu'à 10 milliards de dollars à la Tunisie

original_payload.original_body:

Au menu du Sirexe à Abidjan, les stocks stratégiques pétrolier
Publié le :  24/11/2026 - 00:01
Écouter - 02:13
À Abidjan, le Salon international des ressources extractives et de l’énergie (Sirexe) a fermé ses portes dimanche 22 novembre. Au menu figurait notamment la question des stocks stratégiques pétroliers, ces réserves que les États veulent constituer pour pouvoir répondre pendant un certain temps à la demande en cas de perturbations de l’approvisionnement. Une question importante compte tenu du contexte international incertain, sur laquelle la Côte d’Ivoire entend renforcer ses capacités.
Des visiteurs se rassemblent au Salon international des ressources extractives et de l'énergie (Sirexe) 2026 au Parc des expositions d'Abidjan le 19 novembre 2026.        © Issouf Sanogo / AFP
Publicité
De notre correspondante à Abidjan,
Depuis 1983, la Société de gestion des stocks pétroliers de   Côte d’Ivoire  , appelée Gestoci, est chargée d’administrer les stocks stratégiques du pays. Elle dispose de deux dépôts opérationnels à Abidjan et Yamoussoukro. Mais l’enjeu face au contexte international est aussi de développer les capacités de raffinage. «  Je sais qu’à un moment, les pays n’aimaient pas dévoiler leurs stocks stratégiques, ce n’est pas la Côte d’Ivoire qui va déroger à la règle. Mais ce que je peux vous dire, c’est qu’aujourd’hui, face à la situation à laquelle vous faites allusion, la capacité actuelle de notre raffinerie ne suffit pas  », détaille Mamadou Sangafowa-Coulibaly, ministre des Mines, du Pétrole et de l’Énergie.
«  Nous avons donc prévu de mettre une deuxième raffinerie, pas seulement à cause de la crise, mais parce que   nous voulons raffiner localement   les découvertes de notre propre pays. Parce que l’actuelle raffinerie a été conçue sur le brut du   Nigeria  , qui est un brut lourd. Or nos découvertes sont issues de brut léger, et quand nous allons faire cette raffinerie, nous allons satisfaire les besoins de notre pays et ceux des pays voisins  », précise-t-il encore. En effet, au-delà des stocks de produit fini administrés par la Gestoci, la présence d’une raffinerie à Abidjan permet de stocker du brut et des produits semi-finis.
À lire aussi  Après l’extraction, l’Afrique de l’Ouest mise sur le raffinage de l’or
Stocks et volatilité des prix
«  Le stockage de brut de la SIR  [la Société ivoirienne de raffinage, NDLR]  permet d’avoir du stock au moins pour un mois. Nous traitons un million de barils tous les quinze jours : chaque fois que nous recevons un bateau de brut, nous avons un million en stock  », explique Tiotioho Soro, directeur général de la SIR. «  Donc sur cette question, nous avons un mois d’autonomie sur le brut, la matière première. Ce qui est tout à fait raisonnable, parce qu’avec la volatilité des prix, c’est un peu un risque de faire trop de stock pour une raffinerie  », met-il en avant.
S’il reste des défis comme l’accessibilité des produits stockés, qui sont majoritairement concentrés à Abidjan, la Côte d’Ivoire est plutôt avancée sur la question des stocks stratégiques. Elle garde par ailleurs un rôle important dans la sous-région, puisqu’elle exporte du carburant vers des pays comme le Mali et le Burkina Faso.
À lire aussi  Énergie: après un «choc immense», la guerre au Moyen-Orient laissera un impact durable, selon l’AIE

items.title: Nigeria: les objectifs d’autosuffisance en riz s’éloignent

original_payload.original_title: Nigeria: les objectifs d’autosuffisance en riz s’éloignent
original_payload.original_body:
Nigeria: les objectifs d’autosuffisance en riz s’éloignent
Au Nigeria, le secteur du riz est en perte de vitesse. Selon la presse locale, 90 des 260 rizeries (usines de transformation du riz) ont cessé leurs activités, des données qui recoupent les importations de riz en forte hausse ces dernières années. Un coup dur pour les autorités qui souhaitaient atteindre l'autosuffisance cette année.

1 min     Temps de lecture
Des ouvriers chargent des sacs de riz dans un camion sur un marché de Lagos, au Nigeria, le mardi 7 février 2023.         AP - Sunday Alamba
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Parmi les causes de ce repli figurent l'augmentation des coûts de production due notamment aux prix des engrais – en forte hausse – mais également du diesel dont dépendent les transformateurs.
S'ajoute à cela la fin de programmes tels que l'Anchor Borrowers' Programme qui permettait aux petits producteurs d'assurer les débouchés de leur production ou encore d'obtenir des prêts à taux préférentiels.
Alors que le prix du riz local augmente, le riz importé, lui, est très compétitif et les acteurs du secteur témoignent, cette année, d'une augmentation importante des importations, ce que confirment les chiffres, à savoir 2,1 millions de tonnes importées en 2023, contre plus de 3,6 millions de tonnes en 2026.
Le manque de rentabilité de la production de riz se répercute donc dans les choix des producteurs. Ils délaissent le riz pour se tourner vers le sorgho et le sésame, par exemple. Les rizeries tournent donc largement en dessous de leurs capacités.
Dans son dernier rapport, l’AFEX – la bourse de matières premières agricoles au   Nigeria   – estime que la production de riz pourrait s’effondrer de près de 2 millions de tonnes sur la prochaine campagne de commercialisation.

items.title: Ethiopia Needs Political Reconciliation, Not Another Military Victory

original_payload.original_title: Ethiopia Needs Political Reconciliation, Not Another Military Victory
original_payload.original_body:
Viewpoint
Ethiopia Needs Political Reconciliation, Not Another Military Victory
24 November, 2026
Ermias Amare
SUPPORT ETHIOPIA INSIGHT
What Tibor Nagy’s insights reveal about Ethiopia’s political choices.
Ambassador Tibor Nagy and I go back more than two decades. Our paths crossed long before today’s political debates, through development work, education, and a shared attachment to Ethiopia.
Following the Ethio-Eritrean war, I designed the USAID-funded Doha Resettlement Project. I still remember visiting it with Ambassador Nagy to observe its progress. Those were different days, but they marked the beginning of a relationship and conversations about Ethiopia that have continued for more than twenty years.
Nagy’s contribution to Ethiopia extended beyond conventional diplomacy. During his tenure as U.S. ambassador, he helped strengthen relationships between American and Ethiopian universities. Those partnerships opened doors for young Ethiopian academics, including some of us teaching at Ethiopian universities, to pursue graduate studies in the United States.
I was one of those fortunate beneficiaries.
So was Getachew Reda.
Our paths eventually diverged. Getachew returned home and remained deeply involved in his country’s affairs. I chose the relative comfort and opportunities of building my life and career in the United States.
But physically leaving Ethiopia and emotionally leaving Ethiopia are two different things. Not a day has gone by without my thinking about my motherland. I have continued to follow its triumphs and tragedies, argue about its politics, and write about a country I still deeply care about.
Perhaps that is why Nagy and I have continued talking about Ethiopia all these years.
I have shared a Texas steak with him in Lubbock and had countless conversations about Ethiopia, Africa, Washington, and the complicated politics of the Horn. We agree on much and disagree on important matters. But I have never questioned his affection for Ethiopia.
Nagy served as U.S. ambassador to Ethiopia from 1999 to 2002 and later as assistant secretary of state for African affairs. Having previously  served  at the U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa, he has maintained a close interest in the country long after leaving government.
His experience also gave him an interesting perspective on something many Ethiopians misunderstand: Washington.
In a  recent interview , he joked about the tendency of Ethiopians to imagine that the president of the United States wakes up thinking about Ethiopia and goes to bed thinking about Ethiopia. Sometimes, he said, he simply laughs at that perception.
The point is not that Ethiopia is unimportant. With its enormous population, history, and geopolitical influence, it is a major country in the Horn of Africa. But Washington has interests across the world. Ethiopia is one important file among many.
Ethiopians sometimes interpret every statement from Washington as evidence of a grand strategy designed specifically for or against their country. International politics is usually less romantic than that.
Perhaps that is one reason I continue to listen when Nagy speaks, even when I disagree with him.
A Needless War
Many of Nagy’s views resonate deeply with me. When war  broke out  in northern Ethiopia in November 2020, we were both saddened. Nagy would later  describe  the conflict as “one of the most needless wars in history.”
I couldn’t agree more.
Whatever political calculations existed at the time, the human cost eventually dwarfed whatever objectives the protagonists believed they could achieve.
For years, I kept asking myself: what exactly was the objective? What political goal could justify the lives lost, displacement, destruction of infrastructure, and bitterness among people who ultimately still have to live next to one another?
Even at the beginning of the war, Nagy questioned the TPLF leadership’s objectives. His  assessment  was that the conflict was not about Tigray’s secession but rather about removing Abiy Ahmed and restoring the TPLF’s former prominence in Ethiopian politics.
With hindsight, even many who once sympathized with the TPLF have reassessed those decisions. History will continue debating who did what, when, and why. The dead, however, have no such luxury.
Nagy and I also find common ground on the Nile. His argument to Egypt is straightforward: this is 2026, not the nineteenth or twentieth century.
The political and economic realities of the Nile Basin have changed. Ethiopia can no longer be expected to accept historical arrangements indefinitely while being denied the ability to develop water resources originating within its territory.
Nagy believes recognizing this reality could produce a win-win agreement between Ethiopia and Egypt. That is precisely the approach the region needs.
Egypt’s legitimate concerns about water security deserve respect, as does Ethiopia’s right to development. The Nile should not be treated as a zero-sum contest in which Ethiopia’s development automatically becomes Egypt’s loss. There is enough history between these two ancient civilizations. What they need now is a future.
The same realism should apply to Ethiopia’s search for reliable and diversified access to the sea.
Nagy argues that dependence on a single primary maritime corridor creates genuine economic and strategic vulnerabilities and that Ethiopia has every right to pursue mutually beneficial agreements with neighboring coastal states.
But economic necessity does not confer sovereignty over another country’s coastline. A population of 120 million, or 150 million someday, does not automatically create a legal right to somebody else’s territory.
Ethiopia’s solution must come through diplomacy: negotiated port access, commercial agreements, leases, infrastructure integration, and regional economic cooperation. The objective should not be taking somebody else’s sea, but making geography work for everybody.
Alliances and Interests
Nagy is skeptical of the alliances emerging around Ethiopia. His analysis raises an important question: what holds an alliance together once its common enemy disappears?
That question is particularly relevant to the recently  announced  Alliance for Survival, which brought together the TPLF, a Fano faction, the Oromo Liberation Army, and other groups opposed to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
In his interview with Meaza Mohammed of Roha TV, Nagy described it essentially as an “ alliance on paper .”
Its members may share one immediate objective: opposing Abiy. But a common enemy is not the same as a common vision for Ethiopia.
The contradictions are considerable. The TPLF and Fano were fighting each other only a few years ago, and serious territorial disputes remain unresolved. Their constituencies also hold sharply different views of Ethiopia’s constitutional order. The TPLF has historically defended the multinational federal arrangement it helped establish, while important strands of Amhara political thought have challenged aspects of that system. The OLA brings another political history and set of demands.
Suppose the alliance succeeds in removing Abiy. Then what? How would its members resolve territorial disputes, approach ethnic federalism, settle the constitutional question, and distribute political power?
A common enemy can bring yesterday’s adversaries into the same room. It cannot manufacture a common political philosophy. That is the deeper meaning behind Nagy’s description of an “alliance on paper.” Today’s common enemy does not necessarily create tomorrow’s common vision.
Another Nagy observation that resonates with me is his skepticism toward the phrase “the international community.”
We often speak of the international community as though it were a single government applying one coherent moral standard to the world. No such government exists.
Washington, Beijing, Moscow, Brussels, Cairo, Ankara, Abu Dhabi, and Riyadh all have interests. Sometimes they converge; often they collide.
International institutions such as the United Nations, World Bank, and IMF exert considerable diplomatic and economic influence, but they operate within a system in which powerful states retain disproportionate influence.
For Ethiopia, the lesson is straightforward: foreign policy must be built on interests and relationships, not romantic assumptions about permanent friends or enemies.
Federal Questions
Nagy also challenges political assumptions that have hardened into conventional wisdom. One concerns ethnic federalism.
Some Ethiopian intellectuals speak as though Ethiopia invented the concept of organizing federal units around linguistic or ethnic communities. It did not.
Nagy has pointed to Switzerland, not because the two countries are identical, but because other federal systems have accommodated linguistic and cultural identities. The crucial difference lies in the institutions surrounding them.
As he has essentially argued, Switzerland learned to distribute prosperity, while Ethiopia’s federal system has too often operated amid poverty and intense competition.
The comparison has limits. Ethiopia is not Switzerland. But federalism itself may not be the disease; the institutions surrounding it may be the problem.
I would add an important qualification. Ethnic federalism without genuine democracy can become ethnic competition institutionalized by the state. When citizens believe access to resources, employment, security, and political power depends primarily on which ethnic group controls government, federalism can magnify differences rather than manage them.
Switzerland learned how to share prosperity. Ethiopia too often ended up organizing competition over poverty.
Federalism requires more than drawing boundaries. It requires functioning democratic institutions, economic opportunity, minority protections, and a willingness to lose political power without fearing for one’s existence.
The TPLF’s Future
For all the areas where Nagy and I agree, there is one fundamental issue on which our assessments diverge: the present power and future of the TPLF.
Nagy appears to believe the organization remains sufficiently intact to continue as a major political force and that some form of coexistence with the Prosperity Party remains possible.
I see something fundamentally different.
The TPLF’s greatest loss, in my view, is not military hardware, government offices, or even formal political authority. It is psychological.
For decades, the organization fused three separate ideas into one political identity: the TPLF, Tigray, and the people of Tigray. Criticizing one was often interpreted as criticizing all three.
That monopoly has been broken, and no political force has done more to dismantle it than the people of Tigray themselves.
A population that endured war, displacement, hunger, and enormous loss has every right to question everyone, including the organization that governed Tigray in its name.
The TPLF may retain experienced cadres, networks, loyal supporters, and political influence. But organizational survival is not the same as retaining ownership of a people’s political identity. That era, in my view, is ending.
This is where I believe Ambassador Nagy may eventually revise his assessment. The Tigray he once knew politically has changed profoundly.
Perhaps one day we will have another Texas steak in Lubbock and revisit this conversation. Maybe then I’ll remind him that I told him so.
But rejecting the TPLF’s political monopoly does not mean endorsing the Prosperity Party.
Ethiopians deserve more than a choice between old authoritarianism and new authoritarianism. They deserve peace, constitutional government, accountable institutions, freedom of expression, and a political system in which losing an election does not mean losing one’s security, livelihood, or place in the country.
The federal government bears primary responsibility for protecting Ethiopia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and maintaining lawful public order. But state authority alone does not confer political legitimacy. Legitimacy must be earned.
With economic hardship, armed conflicts, and deep political mistrust across several regions, Ethiopia cannot indefinitely govern its contradictions through force. It needs a credible national dialogue, not a ceremonial conference with predetermined conclusions. It needs reconciliation, accountability, and a political settlement broad enough to allow Ethiopians with fundamentally different views to live under the same constitutional roof.
Other post-conflict societies offer lessons worth studying, but Ethiopia must develop a reconciliation model suited to its own history.
Tigray’s Transition
The political transformation underway in Tigray should not be mistaken for a finished project. The dismantling of the TPLF’s old monopoly has created an opening, but an opening is not yet democracy.
The caretaker administration has an opportunity to demonstrate that political change means more than replacing one group of appointed officials with another.
For decades, power in Tigray was  concentrated  within the ruling structure. Local leaders could be appointed, reshuffled, or sidelined from above, while political survival often depended on loyalty to the organization.
Allowing communities to choose their woreda, kebele, and other local leaders would therefore represent something many have not genuinely experienced for decades: the ability to choose those who govern them.
But the federal government must resist the temptation to replace one political monopoly with another. The Prosperity Party has every right to compete for Tigrayans’ support, but no entitlement to their votes. Political parties and movements across Tigray need space to organize, campaign, and present competing visions.
Otherwise, control of the institutions of the state—the proverbial bank and tank—could reproduce the old problem under a different political logo.
The caretaker administration should remain exactly what its name implies: a caretaker, not the architect of Tigray’s permanent political future.
The question is whether Tigrayans are finally free to decide who represents them. If they choose PP, that choice should be respected. If they choose another organization, that choice must be equally respected. Democracy begins when those who control the state accept that they may not control the outcome.
Recent outreach by federal officials is encouraging. Field Marshal Birhanu Jula’s  visit  to Mekelle and his emphasis on Tigray’s place within Ethiopia are part of a conversation that needs to continue.
Tigray is not a peripheral footnote in Ethiopia’s history. Aksum, Adwa, Gundet, and Dogali are not merely Tigrayan memories; they are woven into the historical consciousness of Ethiopia itself. Separating Tigray’s history from Ethiopia’s would require tearing pages out of the same book.
But historical recognition alone cannot produce reconciliation. It must be accompanied by political inclusion.
The federal government must engage Tigray’s diverse political actors, including those with whom it profoundly disagrees, provided they pursue their objectives peacefully.
Political integration cannot mean political assimilation. Nor should reconciliation require Tigrayans to adopt the federal government’s interpretation of recent history. Their grievances, fears, and political disagreements will not disappear simply because the balance of military power has changed. Those disagreements need somewhere peaceful to go.
From Arms to Politics
The remaining TPLF-aligned armed forces must also confront a changed political reality.
For decades, the TPLF’s power rested on more than its military strength. It commanded an institutional architecture encompassing government, security, local administration, economic networks, and an organizational structure reaching from the highest levels down to local communities.
Much of that architecture has now been dismantled.
Yet  some  within the remaining armed movement appear to believe that retreating to rural areas or mountains and continuing an insurgency could recreate an earlier generation’s political comeback.
Today’s Ethiopia is not the Ethiopia of the 1970s, 1980s, or 1991. Its political environment, technology, military capabilities, and regional circumstances have changed. History does not repeat itself simply because an organization remembers how it once succeeded.
The path toward disarmament, demobilization, and civilian reintegration should remain open. Those willing to put down their weapons should not automatically be treated as permanent enemies.
Subject to accountability for serious crimes and appropriate security safeguards, Ethiopia should pursue credible reintegration mechanisms allowing former combatants to return to civilian life. Where legally and politically appropriate, negotiated amnesty or other transitional arrangements could form part of a broader settlement. Reconciliation, however, must not mean impunity for grave abuses, whoever committed them.
Abandoning armed struggle should not require abandoning political conviction. If the TPLF, or whatever organizations emerge from its remnants, believes it retains a constituency, there is one legitimate way to demonstrate it: go to the people.
Organize peacefully, present a program, build coalitions, debate opponents, and ask Tigrayans for their votes. If they choose you, govern. If they reject you, accept their verdict.
That is the transition Ethiopia needs: from the politics of the gun to the politics of persuasion.
The federal government has an equally important responsibility. It cannot chase former combatants into the mountains while closing peaceful political space in the cities.
A successful transition requires movement from both sides: armed groups must abandon violence, and the state must embrace genuine political inclusion.
The door out of the mountains must lead somewhere: to civilian life, political dialogue, reconciliation, and ultimately the ballot box. That would not erase the past, but it might prevent another generation from having to repeat it.
A Shared Principle
Perhaps this is where Nagy and I ultimately come together. Political organizations come and go. Ethiopia remains.
Those who imagine Ethiopia can simply be Balkanized underestimate the historical, economic, cultural, and human ties binding its peoples together. But those who believe unity can be preserved indefinitely through coercion make an equally dangerous mistake.
A country is strongest when its people choose to remain together, not when they are forced to.
Ethiopia’s future cannot belong exclusively to PP, TPLF, Fano, OLA, or any other political organization. Nor can it belong to one individual. It has to belong to Ethiopians.
After more than twenty years of conversations with Ambassador Nagy, from development projects and university exchanges to Washington politics and Texas steaks in Lubbock, perhaps this is the principle on which we agree most: Ethiopia’s problems are ultimately political, and their lasting solutions must also be political.
Dialogue, compromise, democracy, and reconciliation may lack the excitement of battlefield victories or revolutionary slogans. But after everything Ethiopians have endured, perhaps peaceful political compromise is exactly the revolution the country needs.
Query or correction?  Email us

items.title: Appeals court renews Trump bid for federal jurisdiction in hush-money case

original_payload.original_title: Appeals court renews Trump bid for federal jurisdiction in hush-money case
original_payload.original_body:
A federal appeals court has revived United States President Donald Trump’s bid to transfer his New York criminal hush-money case to federal court,  months  after a district judge rejected the effort for a third time.
On Monday, a three-judge panel of the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a lower court ruling that had  kept the case  in New York state court.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items    list 1 of 4  US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
list 2 of 4  Trump nominates Todd Blanche as US attorney general, teeing up Senate fight
list 3 of 4  Why did Trump fire Pam Bondi from Justice Department, who is Todd Blanche?
list 4 of 4  US judge rejects Trump’s bid to switch hush-money case to federal court
end of list
In a two-page order, the 2nd Circuit panel said it disagreed with the late US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein’s denial of Trump’s request for the “removal” of his case to federal court.
The appeals court said Hellerstein had “erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case” after conviction.
It directed a federal judge in Manhattan to consider whether the proceedings could be brought under federal jurisdiction.
In a written statement provided to The Associated Press news agency, a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said the president “appreciates the 2nd Circuit’s prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System”.
Trump has sought to use presidential immunity in federal court to have his conviction overturned. He was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in 2024, though he has denied any wrongdoing.
Trump’s New York criminal conviction
The case  stems  from a $130,000 “hush money” payment made shortly before the 2016 presidential election to  adult film performer Stormy Daniels .
Daniels had claimed she had an affair with the Republican leader while he was married — an allegation he denies — and prosecutors alleged that the money was intended to buy her silence during a tense campaign season.

items.title: Bukele shares details on deaths of Salvadoran troops in Haiti intervention

original_payload.original_title: Bukele shares details on deaths of Salvadoran troops in Haiti intervention
original_payload.original_body:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has identified the  three soldiers  from his Central American country who were killed while on an anti-gang mission in Haiti.
Late on Sunday, Bukele  posted  on social media that their names were Lieutenant Cristian Daniel Palacios Santos and Corporals Emerson Alexander Zepeda Zelada and Wilber Manuel Serrano Medina.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Why are Bukele’s Salvadoran troops in Haiti and what have they achieved?
list 2 of 3  El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term after constitution change
list 3 of 3  Three Salvadoran soldiers killed in Haiti while handling explosives
end of list
“Tragically, an accidental explosion during that mission claimed their lives,” Bukele said.
He also described instances where the men had shown “bravery” in the past.
During “tests in El Salvador”, Bukele said that Zepeda Zelada and Serrano Medina took quick action to disarm a grenade lodged in a drone.
“It was not possible to steer the drone toward a completely safe area for it to crash,” Bukele said. “They were fully aware of the immense risk they were taking, yet they chose to act to protect others. And they succeeded.”
According to Bukele, Palacios Santos was admired for recently taking control during a “critical moment” in an operation in which some contractors allegedly retreated.
“He acted with speed and determination, managing to save several lives, including those of his own colleagues,” Bukele wrote. “We all applaud his bravery.”
He didn’t identify the contractors.
Bukele also used his post to pledge that Salvadoran troops who want to leave Haiti could do so immediately without facing reprisals.

items.title: Trump calls to ‘expedite’ US federal executions, blasts Gavin Newsom

original_payload.original_title: Trump calls to ‘expedite’ US federal executions, blasts Gavin Newsom
original_payload.original_body:
United States President Donald Trump has reaffirmed his support for the death penalty in an event that doubled as a platform to attack one of his most visible critics, California Governor Gavin Newsom.
On Monday, Trump spoke at the Department of Justice in Washington, DC, where he was joined by the families of crime victims and his attorney general, Todd Blanche.
Recommended Stories

list 2 of 3  California governor commutes sentences of more than 500 people on death row
list 3 of 3  US poll shows death penalty lost majority support for first time since 1971
end of list
“The ultimate crimes deserve the ultimate punishment,” Trump said of the death penalty, calling it a cornerstone of “ virtually every society throughout history, at least every successful society”.
“Under the Trump administration, we are bringing it back, and we will not stop in our pursuit of justice. We will not yield.”
He concluded the appearance by signing a presidential directive ordering the Department of Justice to seek the death penalty in murder cases involving children, rape and human trafficking.
The directive also pushes for the attorney general to “expedite” executions for those on federal death row.
As part of his speech, Trump called on Congress to pass the Just Punishment for Murder Act, a bill sponsored by Republican Representative Brandon Gill, which the president said would “strengthen the death penalty in America”.
But he dedicated much of his remarks to slamming Newsom, a Democrat widely seen as a possible contender for the 2028 presidential race.
Newsom’s second term as governor will end on January 4. Under California term limits, he was ineligible to run again in the 2026 midterm elections.
Still, the governor and former San Francisco mayor has carved a national profile for himself as a proxy for Democrats during high-stakes political campaigns — and as a critic of Trump.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s dramatic  return to the helm  of the world’s most valuable chipmaker, less than two weeks after his resignation, has sent the company’s stock soaring.
At the same time, the White House’s involvement in his reinstatement has raised questions about Silicon Valley’s growing sway in Washington, with United States President Donald Trump claiming to have been a linchpin in the decision.

What happened?
The saga began less than two weeks ago when Huang resigned amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Beijing has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. She previously led Megaspeed, a company that had a business relationship with Nvidia, the Santa Clara, California-based tech giant.
Nvidia’s board had begun an investigation into the allegations, but Huang resigned before it reached a conclusion.

items.title: FG’s oil revenue tumbles N1.44tn despite price boom

original_payload.original_title: FG’s oil revenue tumbles N1.44tn despite price boom
original_payload.original_body:
The Federal Government recorded a N1.44tn decline in gross oil revenue in the first half of 2026 despite a 41.23 per cent increase in international crude oil prices in the second quarter of the year, according to the Budget Office of the Federation.
An analysis of the Second Quarter and Half-Year 2026 Budget Implementation Report showed that gross oil revenue fell to N7.88tn between January and June 2026, compared with approximately N9.32tn recorded during the corresponding period of 2025.
The decline represented a 15.45 per cent year-on-year contraction, highlighting Nigeria’s continued difficulty in translating favourable international oil prices into higher government revenue.
The report, prepared by the Budget Office under the Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, disclosed that the N7.88tn collected during the first six months of 2026 was also N10.78tn below the government’s half-year revenue target of N18.65tn.

For years, cryptocurrency discussions across Africa have largely focused on trading and speculation. What has changed to suggest that the greater opportunity now lies in the underlying infrastructure supporting financial transactions?
I think what has changed is that we are beginning to understand where the real economic value of digital assets lies.

Partager

La chanteuse iranienne Parastoo Ahmadi et quatre collaborateurs ont chacun reçu 74 coups de fouet lundi 23 novembre à Qom, après la confirmation en appel d’une condamnation liée à un concert diffusé en ligne sans le voile obligatoire.
L’exécution de la peine a eu lieu au service chargé de l’application des décisions du parquet de Qom, selon l’avocat Mostafa Nili, cité par le média iranien Emtedad. Les quatre autres condamnés sont Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia et Mohsen Lashkari, membres de l’équipe artistique et technique du concert.
La branche 16 de la cour d’appel de la province de Qom avait confirmé le jugement rendu par la branche 122 du tribunal pénal. Les cinq artistes avaient également été frappés d’une interdiction de deux ans d’exercer une activité artistique ou musicale et d’une interdiction de quitter le territoire pendant la même durée.
Le dossier remonte à décembre 2024. Parastoo Ahmadi avait enregistré avec plusieurs musiciens une prestation au caravansérail historique de Deir Gachin, près de Qom. Le concert, réalisé sans public, avait été mis en ligne sur YouTube. La chanteuse y apparaissait sans le voile imposé aux femmes en Iran.
Cette diffusion avait déclenché l’ouverture d’une procédure pour « atteinte à la décence publique » par la production et la diffusion de contenus qualifiés d’« obscènes » par l’accusation. Parastoo Ahmadi et plusieurs musiciens avaient été arrêtés en décembre 2024 avant d’être libérés sous caution.
Âgée de 29 ans, la chanteuse avait contesté les poursuites avec les autres prévenus. Le rejet de leur appel, à la fin du mois de septembre, avait rendu la peine exécutoire.

Amnesty International a choisi Rokiatou Doumbia, commerçante et influenceuse malienne surnommée « Rose Vie Chère », parmi les figures de sa campagne mondiale Écrire pour les droits. L’organisation a annoncé lundi 23 novembre qu’elle mobiliserait ses membres à partir du 10 décembre pour réclamer sa libération immédiate et sans condition.
Âgée de 48 ans et mère de deux enfants, Rokiatou Doumbia compte environ 175 000 abonnés sur TikTok. Elle s’est fait connaître par ses prises de parole sur la hausse des prix alimentaires et les difficultés quotidiennes des ménages. Amnesty souligne également son engagement associatif auprès de femmes et ses distributions de nourriture.
L’influenceuse a été arrêtée le 13 mars 2023 après une intervention sur TikTok, puis à la radio, dans laquelle elle critiquait le coût de la vie et les autorités de transition. Elle avait d’abord été poursuivie pour incitation à la révolte et trouble à l’ordre public. Deux chefs supplémentaires, atteinte au crédit de l’État et association de malfaiteurs, ont été ajoutés le 29 mars.
Le 2 août 2023, elle avait été condamnée à un an de prison et à une amende d’un million de francs CFA. En janvier 2024, la cour d’appel a écarté les premières poursuites, mais son maintien en détention s’est poursuivi dans le cadre des deux chefs ajoutés après son arrestation.
Le 17 août 2026, la chambre criminelle de la cour d’appel de Bamako l’a condamnée à dix ans de prison, dont trois avec sursis, pour atteinte au crédit de l’État et association de malfaiteurs. Elle a été jugée lors de la même procédure que l’activiste Mohamed Youssouf Bathily, dit  Ras Bath , qui a reçu la même peine.
La mobilisation annoncée prévoit l’envoi de lettres, de courriels, de cartes et de pétitions. La chargée de campagne Khadidiatou Diaw appelle les autorités maliennes à libérer Rokiatou Doumbia et Ras Bath immédiatement et sans condition.
Écrire pour les droits fête cette année sa 25e édition. Selon Amnesty, la campagne a suscité plus de 50 millions d’actions depuis 2001 et contribué à améliorer la situation de plus d’une centaine de personnes défendues dans le monde.

23/11/2026    par    Saturnin Bossa
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Le boxeur britannique  Tyson Fury,  37 ans, affirme avoir reçu un diagnostic de schizophrénie, selon un communiqué publié lundi 23 novembre 2026 par  Netflix . L’ancien champion du monde des poids lourds situe ce diagnostic juste après sa victoire de 2015 face à  Wladimir Klitschko , puis évoque un trouble bipolaire identifié en 2017. Le documentaire  Tyson Fury  sort vendredi 27 novembre, deux semaines avant son combat contre  Anthony Joshua  à Cardiff, au  Royaume-Uni.
« Les mots ne peuvent pas expliquer les ténèbres dans lesquelles je me trouvais. Je venais de la version vivante des abîmes de l’enfer. Et à 100 %, je pensais parfois que je finirais dans une chambre capitonnée, porte verrouillée, et ça m’a tellement fait peur. Je me réveillais la nuit comme ça, l’anxiété me paralysait. Je n’arrivais tout simplement pas à la surmonter » , a déclaré  Tyson Fury . Ses propos s’appuient sur un parcours déjà marqué par la maladie, puisqu’il avait abandonné en 2016 ses ceintures WBO, WBA et IBO en invoquant des problèmes de santé mentale, avant de remonter sur le ring en 2018.
Le film réunit aussi des témoignages de son épouse Paris Fury et de son père  John Fury , ainsi que des images d’archives inédites. Il ne précise pas comment la maladie est suivie aujourd’hui.

Leur volume total s’établit à  32,03 millions de litres , dont  20,69 millions de litres de gasoil  et  11,34 millions de litres de supercarburant . Un club de Ligue 2 veut attirer Cyril Hanouna dans son capital
23/11/2026    par    Amos Traoré
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Du paysage audiovisuel au monde du football, il n’y a qu’un pas et  Cyril Hanouna  pourrait en être l’illustration. En effet, d’après des sources concordantes, le célèbre animateur pourrait bientôt faire son retour dans l’univers du football. En effet, l’on apprend qu’Hanouna a été approché par le club de  Guingamp  pour entrer au capital du club.
Le mythique club français  qui a révélé de grands talents occupe présentement la 12e place de  Ligue 2 . Pour assurer son avenir sur le long terme, l’En Avant souhaite attirer de nouveaux investisseurs.. Une rencontre entre les deux parties est envisagée en fin de semaine. Si les discussions aboutissent, Cyril Hanouna aura frappé un grand coup, lui qui a déjà tenté une expérience dans la gestion d’une équipe de football.
Un retour dans le football après l’expérience marseillaise
La possible arrivée du sulfureux animateur dans le capital de Guingamp fait beaucoup parler. Dans un passé récent, le quadragénaire avait investi aux côtés de l’ex international sénégalais  Souleymane Diawara  dans le projet de  l’Athlético Marseille.  Malheureusement, l’expérience n’a pas été du tout concluante et le projet fut un échec.
L’En Avant Guingamp ce n’est pas l’Athlético Marseille. Le club figure en bonne place dans l’histoire du football hexagonal. L’équipe bretonne a remporté deux coupes de France et a révélé des superstars comme  Didier Drogba  et  Florent Malouda . Si Hanouna devient actionnaire du club, il aura la possibilité de s’impliquer dans un projet ambitieux à long terme. Même si l’opération est en bonne voie, il n’y a pas encore d’accord définitif. Les discussions se poursuivent et les choses pourraient se décanter dans les jours à venir. Dès lors, on saura ce que Cyril Hanouna peut apporter comme plus value à un club du statut de Guingamp.

items.title: Donald Trump veut exiger la peine de mort pour les meurtriers d'enfants

original_payload.original_title: Donald Trump veut exiger la peine de mort pour les meurtriers d'enfants
original_payload.original_body:
Photo : rawpixel
Donald Trump veut exiger la peine de mort pour les meurtriers d'enfants
23/11/2026    par    Charly Hessoun
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Le président américain  Donald Trump  a annoncé lundi 23 novembre 2026 qu’il signera une directive imposant au ministère de la Justice de requérir la peine capitale contre les meurtriers d’enfants. La mesure vise aussi les violeurs et les trafiquants d’êtres humains qui tuent leurs victimes. Il s’exprimait au siège du ministère, à Washington, aux côtés du procureur général  Todd Blanche  et du directeur du FBI  Kash Patel , un jour où il attaquait directement le gouverneur de Californie.
« Je signerai une directive présidentielle ordonnant au ministère de la Justice de requérir la peine de mort contre les meurtriers d’enfants, ainsi que contre les violeurs et les trafiquants d’êtres humains qui tuent leurs victimes. Mon décret demande aussi au procureur général d’accélérer l’exécution des condamnations à mort fédérales » , a déclaré  Donald Trump.
Ainsi, la directive vise des crimes où la victime est morte. Or la jurisprudence de la Cour suprême interdit la peine capitale pour les crimes sans mort de victime, ce qui explique cette limite. Le décret signé le 20 janvier 2025 demandait déjà au procureur général de requérir la peine de mort pour tous les crimes d’une gravité qui l’exige, sans mentionner le viol ni le trafic d’enfants.
Cette annonce survient alors que  Gavin Newsom  a proposé le 5 novembre de commuer en perpétuité les 548 condamnations à mort de son État.  « Le gouverneur Newsom abandonne les victimes et leurs familles en refusant de rendre justice face à ces barbares qui ont tué des enfants » , a réagi la porte-parole de la Maison-Blanche,  Lauren Bis .

items.title: L'Iran menace de frapper les bases américaines en Europe en cas d'attaque

original_payload.original_title: L'Iran menace de frapper les bases américaines en Europe en cas d'attaque
original_payload.original_body:
Photo d'illustration LNT
L'Iran menace de frapper les bases américaines en Europe en cas d'attaque
23/11/2026    par    Charly Hessoun
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
L’Iran  a désigné lundi 23 novembre 2026 les bases américaines du  Royaume-Uni,  d’ Allemagne  et de  Bulgarie  comme des cibles possibles si Washington s’en sert pour l’attaquer.  « Une base américaine au Royaume-Uni, en Allemagne ou en Bulgarie ne diffère pas pour nous d’une base américaine à Bahreïn. Si les États-Unis utilisent le territoire d’un pays pour mener des opérations contre l’Iran, ce territoire peut devenir une cible de frappes de représailles » , a déclaré  Abbas Moqtadaei , vice-président de la commission parlementaire de la sécurité nationale et de la politique étrangère, à l’agence iranienne SNN.
En effet, le même discours avait déjà été tenu le 11 novembre par le secrétaire du Conseil suprême de sécurité nationale,  Mohsen Rezaï , sur une télévision libanaise.  « Si des avions américains décollent d’une base américaine, même située dans un pays européen ou dans une autre région lointaine, pour bombarder l’Iran, nous frapperons aussi ces bases » , avait-il affirmé. Ainsi, les deux responsables fixent la même règle : la présence d’une base n’expose pas un pays, c’est l’usage qui en est fait. Toutefois  Moqtadaei  siège au Parlement et ne s’exprime pas au nom du gouvernement.
La Bulgarie déjà avertie en juillet
Par la suite, la Bulgarie avait reçu un avertissement direct de Téhéran. Le porte-parole de la diplomatie iranienne,  Esmaïl Baghaï , avait demandé à Sofia de ne pas laisser son territoire servir de point de départ à des opérations contre  l’Iran . Il avait prévenu que le pays deviendrait complice de  « l’agression et des crimes de guerre » . De plus, l’armée américaine utilise la base aérienne de Bezmer, dans ce pays, pour soutenir ses avions ravitailleurs, ce qui l’expose davantage aux menaces iraniennes.
Bahreïn, cible de plusieurs attaques revendiquées
Pour sa part,  Bahreïn  sert de point de comparaison à Moqtadaei, car l’île a été visée à plusieurs reprises ces derniers jours. Les Gardiens de la révolution affirment avoir lancé six drones contre un radar américain de la base de Riffa le 15 novembre. Ils avaient déjà revendiqué le 13 novembre une frappe contre un radar d’alerte avancée, mais l’armée américaine a démenti que l’installation ait été touchée. Elle dit avoir intercepté deux drones, sans dégâts ni victimes. Enfin, l’île abrite le quartier général de la Ve flotte américaine et avait déjà été frappée dans les premières heures de la guerre, le 28 février.

original_payload.original_body:
L'armée algérienne. Photo : DR
Drogue en Algérie : après Tebboune, le chef d’état-major avertit les réseaux criminels
23/11/2026    par    Gildas Amoussou
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Lundi 23 novembre 2026, le général d’armée  Saïd Chanegriha  a lancé une mise en garde directe aux réseaux qui tentent d’inonder  l’Algérie  de stupéfiants. Lors d’une visite au Commandement de la Gendarmerie nationale, il a dénoncé les traîtres qui cherchent à submerger le pays de drogues et de psychotropes, et affirmé que l’État leur opposera sa fermeté.
Ce message fait écho aux propos du président   Abdelmadjid Tebboune  , dimanche 15 novembre, à l’ouverture de l’année judiciaire à la Cour suprême. Il a affirmé que  « c’est une guerre déclarée contre l’Algérie »,  décrivant l’afflux de drogue comme «  une véritable guerre contre notre peuple et notre jeunesse  ». Il a aussi évoqué une riposte : «  Si nécessaire, nous pouvons aller plus loin, jusqu’à la source même de la production de drogue, en légitime défense.  » La principale opération signalée après ce discours est celle du 20 novembre près de la frontière ouest, dans le secteur militaire de Naâma, où deux contrebandiers marocains ont été tués et plus de 50 kg de kif saisis.
Une exigence de fermeté face aux trafiquants
Saïd Chanegriha  a rappelé devant les gendarmes, que leur corps doit appliquer la loi à tous. «  Aucun individu, ni partie, ne saurait jouir d’une immunité  », a-t-il insisté, ajoutant qu’«  aucune forme de dépassement à l’encontre du citoyen ne saurait être tolérée  », car le citoyen représente «  le socle de l’Etat et de la République, et la source de légitimité de leurs pouvoirs  ». Il a demandé d’intensifier les efforts pour imposer l’autorité de l’État face aux «  tentatives des ennemis de la Patrie et des traîtres d’inonder notre pays par toutes sortes de drogues et de psychotropes  ».
Enfin, il a appelé à  « faire preuve davantage de vigilance et de prudence, pour faire échouer tous les plans malveillants visant notre pays  », et à garantir «  la sécurisation totale et globale »  des régions et des frontières, «  à l’aune de la conjoncture instable que connait notre environnement régional  ». Aussi, il a rappelé, en citant le président, «  l’attachement ferme et constant au devoir de se soumettre tous à la loi, sans exception  ».

Lors d’une visite au Commandement de la Gendarmerie nationale, il a dénoncé les traîtres qui cherchent à submerger le pays de drogues et de psychotropes, et affirmé que l’État leur opposera ... SITUATION OVERVIEW
In October 2026, after receiving initial reports of children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in Deir ez-Zor Governorate, Syria, the Ministry of Health (MoH) mounted a swift response, in coordination with partners.
Conflict, displacement, interrupted immunization and population movement have created immunity gaps. An unrelated variant VDPV1 detection was reported in wastewater in the area in February 2026.
HIGHLIGHTS
The MoH, supported by WHO,UNICEF and partners, is leading the outbreak response, including intensified surveillance and vaccination.
Emergency vaccination activities reached:
34 720 children in October 2026
54 382 in November 2026 (111% of the target of 49 000)
The high coverage can be attributed to population movement. Additional efforts are needed to determine target population in future rounds.
The next campaign is planned for 30 November 2026 in six districts of Deir ez-Zor Governorate, integrating child nutrition assessments, drinking-water chlorine level checks and chlorine distribution.
An expanded scope will follow in December 2026.
The risk of further spread within Syria and to neighbouring countries, including Iraq, remains a concern due to uneven vaccination coverage and immunity gaps, particularly among displaced, mobile and underserved populations.
COORDINATION OF THE RESPONSE
The MoH is coordinating national and subnational actors. WHO and UNICEF are mobilizing regional and global technical expertise, while the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) provides technical and financial support. World Vision and the International Rescue Committee funded the first two vaccination rounds in October and November 2026.
Two coordination meetings involving national, regional and global response teams have reviewed the situation and agreed on priorities. The MoH Incident Management Team meets weekly through its Emergency Operations Centre. The remaining 13 governorates in Syria have been advised to intensify surveillance and preparedness. Cross-border coordination is particularly important for Iraq, given population movements and the history of wild poliovirus transmission across this border in 2013.

Under the Regional Response to Climate Displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa (RE2CLID) program, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is implementing activities across eight districts in Malawi: Blantyre, Blantyre City, Chikwawa, Dowa, Mangochi, Mulanje, Nsanje and Phalombe. The district profiles bring together available data on population, climate hazards, displacement, vulnerability and local capacities in Chikwawa and will be complemented by the forthcoming RE2CLID Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) baseline assessment.
This profile is focused on Chikwawa District, which has experienced recurrent climate-related displacement associated with floods, tropical storms, cyclones and drought. The five Traditional Authorities (TAs) targeted by RE2CLID – Ngabu, Lundu, Makhwira, Maseya and Ngowe – were home to 348,079 people according to the 2018 Census, representing approximately 62 per cent of the district's population.
Historical DTM assessments show that these TAs also accounted for a high proportion of displacement recorded during major flood and storm events: approximately 94 per cent during the 2015 floods, 99 per cent during Cyclone Idai and 89 per cent following Cyclone Freddy. Patterns nevertheless varied between events. Displacement was concentrated particularly in TA Lundu during the 2015 floods and Cyclone Idai, while following Cyclone Freddy, DTM recorded 111,864 IDPs across 43 sites, with the largest shares located in TA Ngabu and TA Makhwira.
Looking ahead, the 2026/27 outlook points to a multi-hazard context. Under the DCCMS Strong El Niño scenario, Chikwawa is classified as extreme drought risk, while extreme-rainfall risk increases from no threat during October–December 2026 to extreme during January–March 2027. Understanding how historical displacement patterns intersect with current and projected climate risks can help inform anticipatory action, preparedness and targeted displacement monitoring.

In late 2015, IOM launched a Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Flow Monitoring system, aiming to monitor Mixed Migration Flows to Europe by land and sea. Since then, DTM gathers, validates and disseminates information on migrants and refugees entering Europe through four main routes:
Eastern Mediterranean route (EMR) : arrivals by sea and land to Bulgaria, Cyprus and Greece
Central Mediterranean route (CMR) : arrivals by sea to Italy and Malta
Western Mediterranean route (WMR) : arrivals by sea to the Peninsular Coasts of Spain, Balearic Islands, by land to the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla
Western African Atlantic route (WAAR) : arrivals by sea to the Canary Islands of Spain
DTM also monitors data on migrants in transit through the  Western Balkan route (WBR) , including data from Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Kosovo (UNSCR 1244, 1999). These are considered separately to prevent, to the extent possible, the double counting of the same people, crossing multiple borders. Finally, DTM compiles data on migrants entering Croatia, Romania and Slovenia by land, typically after having crossed the Western Balkans or Bulgaria.
This report presents the latest available data and trends, focusing on the third quarter of 2026 and comparing it with the same period in 2025.
In the third quarter of 2026 (Q3 2026), 36,097 migrants arrived in Europe via these four routes. This represents a 42 per cent increase from previous Q2 2026 and a 24 per cent decline compared with Q3 2025. The steepest year-on-year drop was on the CMR (down 59%), followed by the EMR (down 13%). Arrivals were distributed across the CMR to Italy and Malta (24%), the EMR to Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria (42%), the WMR to Spain (25%), and the WAAR to Spain (9%).
According to Eurostat, EU+ countries registered over 99,385 new asylum applications in the third quarter of 2026. Although data on asylum applications remain incomplete at the time of writing, France, Italy and Greece are among the highest ranking countries in the EU27+ in Q3 of 2026. Notably, France registered nearly twice as many first-time asylum applications (27,910) than Italy (15,450) did. Between July and September 2026, the main applicants held nationalities from Afghanistan (10%), Bangladesh (7%) and Sudan (6%), comprising nearly a quarter of all applications registered. These groups are followed by Türkiye, and Pakistan, Ukraine, Syrian Arab Republic and Somalia, averaging at around 4 per cent, respectively.
According to IOM’s MMP, 920 migrants died or went missing at sea while trying to reach Europe through the Mediterranean and Western African Atlantic routes in Q3 of 2026. Of these, 141 perished on the Central Mediterranean, and 350 while trying to cross the Atlantic to reach the Canary Islands. This represents a 6 per cent increase compared to Q3 2025 (871).

Following Cyclone Freddy in 2023, DTM recorded 65,185 internally displaced persons across 27 sites, distributed across most TAs in Nsanje District.

Under the DCCMS Strong El Niño scenario, Nsanje is classified at extreme drought risk, while extreme-rainfall risk increases from no threat during October–December 2026 to extreme during January–March 2027. Understanding how historical displacement patterns intersect with current and projected climate risks can help inform anticipatory action, preparedness and targeted displacement monitoring.

IOM Yemen DTM’s Rapid Displacement Tracking (RDT) tool collects data on estimated numbers of households forced to flee on a daily basis from their locations of origin or displacement, allowing for regular reporting of new displacements in terms of estimated numbers, geography, and needs. It also tracks returnees who returned to their location of origin.
From 1 January to 21 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 65,427 households (HH) (392,562 Individuals) who experienced displacement at least once.
Between 15 and 21 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 2622 households (15732 individuals) displaced at least once. The majority of people moved into/within the following governorates and districts:
Lahj (1589 HHs) – Tuban (1057 HHs), Tur Al Bahah (302 HHs), Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (90 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
Ta’iz (401 HHs) – Sabir Al Mawadim (71 HHs), Jabal Habashi (70 HHs), Ash Shamayatayn (67 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
Aden (382 HHs) – Al Burayqah (295 HHs), Dar Sad (84 HHs), Kritar - Sirah (3 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Lahj.
The majority of people moved from the following governorates and districts:
Lahj (1732 HHs) – Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (1139 HHs), Tur Al Bahah (459 HHs), Al Maqatirah (122 HHs) districts.
Ta’iz (750 HHs) – Al Misrakh (130 HHs), Jabal Habashi (122 HHs), Al Makha (93 HHs) districts.
Al Hodeidah (81 HHs) – Al Khukhah (45 HHs), Hays (28 HHs), Al Hawak (2 HHs) districts.
IOM identified 442 additional households displaced in the previous reporting period, which covered 08 - 14 November 2026, in the governorates of Aden (178 HHs), Abyan (98 HHs), Ma’rib (76 HHs), Ad Dali (41 HHs), Al Maharah (35 HHs), and Hadramawt (14 HHs). These figures have been added to the cumulative displacement total recorded since the beginning of the year.

The findings, interpretations, and conclusions expressed in this update do not necessarily reflect the views of the World Bank, its Board of Executive Directors, or the governments they represent.
KEY MESSAGES
Global food and nutrition security remains fragile amid high costs, climate risks, and trade disruptions. Prices have eased since October but remain above last year's levels because of transport costs and continued logistical constraints. The World Bank projects that food prices willrise 10.3 percentin 2026 and 7.2 percent in 2027.
Food insecurity remains a widespread problem in regions facing conflict and weather-related shocks. Critical situations persist in Somalia, South Sudan, and Sudan, where credible risks of famine remain. In Yemen, 18.3 million people face acute food insecurity amid conflict, displacement, and drought, and there is a credible risk of famine in Ta'izz City if the siege tightens.
A very strong El Niño expected through early 2027 is threatening harvests; flooding in eastern Africa; drought in Southern Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Sahel; and crop losses in Central America. The most severe food insecurity typically emerges in the lean season that follows El Niño–induced rainfall anomalies. Effects vary by region and depend on rainfall patterns, markets, and countries’ capacity to respond.
