items.title: Bangladesh: Clean hands, healthier lives: How one family champions hygiene in Cox’s Bazar

original_payload.original_title: Bangladesh: Clean hands, healthier lives: How one family champions hygiene in Cox’s Bazar
original_payload.original_body:
Bangladesh
+ 1 more
Clean hands, healthier lives: How one family champions hygiene in Cox’s Bazar
Format
News and Press Release
Source
IFRC
Posted
24 Nov 2026
Originally published
24 Nov 2026
Origin
View original
“I had five children when we came to this camp nine years ago, and later another child was born here. All of them fall sick every now and then. There were skin diseases and diarrhoea all the time.”
These are the words of Jomjoma, 45, a resident of the displacement camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, where over 1.2 million Rohingya displaced from Rakhine State in Myanmar are now sheltering across 33 camps.
Severe overcrowding defines daily life. Shelters are packed tightly along narrow pathways on hilly ground, leaving little living space, and dirt and germs can spread quickly.
Jomjoma lives here with her husband, Mohammad Siddik, 61, and their six children. The family has called the camp home for nine years, and illness has been a regular concern.
For families like theirs, the simplest hygiene practices can mean the difference between health and life-threatening illness.
To protect communities from waterborne diseases, the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), together with partners, have worked hand in hand with camp residents since the onset of the crisis, delivering billions of litres of safe water, distributing essential hygiene supplies, and conducting vital household awareness campaigns.
A daily struggle for health in displacement
Life in the early years of displacement was difficult. The family had to collect water from ponds and canals located far from their shelter.
“There was no clean water nearby,”  Siddik said.  “We had to collect water from ponds and canals that were quite far from here. In this hilly area, it was very exhausting and time-consuming, especially for families with children and the elderly. But then, the Red Cross and Red Crescent began providing tap stands in the camps, and one was set up near our house. That made our life much easier.”
From awareness sessions to household champions
Access to safe water was only one part of the transformation. Red Crescent community volunteers regularly visited households throughout the camps, and shared information on the importance of handwashing with soap, safe water storage, and maintaining personal hygiene.
And Jomjoma remembers those visits very clearly.  “The volunteers explained why we should wash our hands before eating, before preparing food, after using the toilet, and after cleaning children. They also invited us to awareness sessions in the facilities. We attended those sessions and learned many things.”
The lessons did not stop at the training centres. After returning home, Siddik and Jomjoma shared what they had learned with their children and neighbours, becoming advocates for healthy practices in their very own community.
“We taught our children the same things the volunteers taught us,” Siddik explained. “Now they know when and how to wash their hands properly.”
The impact has been significant.  “We have fewer instances of falling sick now,”  Jomjoma continued. “It saves money as well because we do not need to visit doctors as often.”
The critical role of WASH in camp environments
Washing hands is one of the simplest yet most effective ways to prevent disease. Yet for millions of people living in dire humanitarian settings, clean water and hygiene materials remain difficult to access. In the displacement camps of Cox’s Bazar, limited resources and overcrowded living conditions continue to challenge efforts to keep communities healthy.
Despite these challenges, the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society and IFRC, with the support of partners, have continued to promote safe hygiene practices among camp residents. As of June 2026, more than 500,000 hygiene and soap kits have been distributed, while more than 240,000 people have received support with safe water services. And since the onset of the crisis in 2017, nearly 6.89 billion litres of safe drinking water have also been provided to more than 95,000 people, helping families reduce the risks of waterborne diseases and improve their overall well-being.
Siddik and Jomjoma are among those receiving these services.Like most people in the camp, Siddik has no formal way of earning a living; here and there, he is hired for daily labour by aid organisations still operating in the camps.
“The camp environment is crowded and muddy, and we get dirty all the time,”  Jomjoma explained.  “If someone goes outside and comes back home, they need to wash their hands and legs thoroughly.”
"When we first arrived here, we did not have much idea about handwashing,”  Siddik recalled and Jomjoma nodded along as she reflected on those early experiences.
Funding cuts threaten health gains
While awareness and behaviour have improved, new challenges are emerging. Like many families in the camps, Siddik and Jomjoma are concerned about receiving fewer hygiene supplies than before.
“Previously, we received more soap from aid organisations,”  Siddik said.  “Now we receive less, but we need soap every day. We use them because we understand its importance.”
For hygiene promotion volunteers and staff members, the concerns raised by families are understandable. Years of awareness campaigns have helped communities adopt healthy habits, but sustaining those habits requires continued access to essential hygiene items.
Nabanita Barua, Senior Water, Sanitation & Hygiene (WASH) Officer at the Bangladesh Red Crescent, warned that funding reductions are severely affecting humanitarian operations.
“Due to funding cuts, we have had to reduce the support to the host communities, including the distribution of some essential hygiene materials such as soap, where these people are equally vulnerable. New arrivals are also a concern. Many have not yet been fully included in hygiene promotion activities, which increase the risk of disease outbreaks, including skin infections and potentially life-threatening acute watery diarrhea.”
Despite these pressures, positive changes have already been observed across many communities in the camps.
“Over the past two years, we have seen a significant reduction in cases of acute watery diarrhea in areas where handwashing practices have improved and people have better access to safe water. Community engagement, hygiene promotion, and reliable water services have played a crucial role in protecting public health,”  says Barua.
Local solutions to sustain essential hygiene supplies
Since 2023, the Bangladesh Red Crescent and IFRC have distributed soap to Rohingya households in the camps, with each family receiving one bar per member every month. This is how Siddik and Jomjoma’s household gets its soap.
One of the ways to manage this demand for soap was to introduce soap production training in the camps. The very first series of trainings saw 80 female participants in total, with the first session taking place in July this year with 30 participants. All participants also received 360 BDT (~ USD 2.92) to help them with their soap-making efforts. Some will use it for their own consumption, while others may sell some off.
For Siddik and Jomjoma, safe water close to home, soap in the household and the knowledge to use it well have meant fewer illnesses, lower medical costs and children who know how to protect themselves.
Their story shows what communities can achieve when the right support reaches them, and why that support must continue, so the healthy habits families have worked so hard to adopt are not lost.
Want to know more about how IFRC supports communities through water, sanitation and hygiene? Click  here .

original_payload.original_title: World: Speed, Scale and Disregard: How new technology and changing tactics are driving civilian harm
original_payload.original_body:

Authors: Jenny McAvoy I Chris Rogers I Emanuela Gillard
War is changing. The risks to civilians are changing with it. From the destruction of critical civilian infrastructure to the growing use of drones and AI-assisted targeting systems, evolving patterns of warfare are exposing civilians to devastating and far-reaching harm.
Drawing on research across six contexts where the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) supports people affected by displacement, this report examines how and why civilians are being harmed - and what can be done to protect them.
Across the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gaza, the Islamic Republic of Iran, Lebanon, Sudan and Ukraine, it identifies two particularly concerning trends: the widespread destruction of infrastructure, disrupting access to essential services, and the growing use of emerging military technologies, raising new challenges for civilian protection and compliance with international humanitarian law. Much of the resulting suffering is foreseeable and can be prevented or reduced.
Reversing this trajectory requires action from parties to conflict and the states that support them. The report calls for greater use of political, military and economic leverage to strengthen compliance with international humanitarian law and efforts to mitigate civilian harm; improved military practices and oversight; earlier investment in restoring damaged civilian infrastructure; and better documentation and analysis of civilian harm to inform efforts to protect civilians.

items.title: Afghanistan: Enough Room to Return? Where 7.2 million Afghan returnees settled, and whether public health services, rentals, and wages can accommodate them

original_payload.original_title: Afghanistan: Enough Room to Return? Where 7.2 million Afghan returnees settled, and whether public health services, rentals, and wages can accommodate them
original_payload.original_body:
Afghanistan
+ 2 more
Enough Room to Return? Where 7.2 million Afghan returnees settled, and whether public health services, rentals, and wages can accommodate them
Format
Assessment
Source
Data for Afghanistan
Posted
23 Nov 2026
Originally published
23 Nov 2026
Attachments
Download Report
(PDF | 1.87 MB)
Author: Ahmad Zia Wahdat, PhD
Between 2021 and October 2026, about 7.2 million Afghans returned from Iran, Pakistan and elsewhere, and one in seven people now living in Afghanistan is a returnee. This independent report by Data for Afghanistan places every returnee in one of Afghanistan's 401 districts. It then measures that number against the people, inhabited land, public health workers, wages, rent and prices already there. It draws only on open and publicly accessible data from IOM, UNHCR, the Ministry of Public Health, WFP and the National Statistics and Information Authority. It introduces a district typology that separates two kinds of pressure: the returnee share of residents and spatial crowding (returnees per km² of inhabited land). The report also includes a stress test for a further one million returnees, recommendations for organizations, and profiles of all 34 provinces with district-level tables.
Return is highly concentrated. Ten districts hold 21% of all returnees, and in Kunduz, Daykundi and Herat close to one resident in four is a returnee. In "saturated" districts, both the returnee share and crowding are above the national average, and 45% of returnees live in these districts. Nationally, there are 252 returnees for every public health worker, and more than 550 in Takhar and Kunduz. Yet new public health facilities over the past five years mostly opened elsewhere. In no province can one unskilled wage keep a returnee household of 6.1 members above the poverty line: it covers only 37% to 76%. Rent for a modest four-bedroom house takes up to 33 days of unskilled wage a month. About 2.7 million returnees are of school age, and half of returnee children aged 5 to 14 are not in education, mainly because of cost and the need for children to work. If one million more people return following the 2026 pattern, Nangarhar, Herat and Kabul would receive 46% of them. Holding today's ratios would then need at least 537 more health workers and 65 more public health facilities.
The report is available in English, Dari and Pashto, with interactive web pages:

items.title: Afghanistan: Keynote remarks of SRSG Patten at the 2026 HearUs Summit: Afghan Women’s Leadership in Achieving Justice and Peace through Accountability, 23 November 2026, Madrid

original_payload.original_title: Afghanistan: Keynote remarks of SRSG Patten at the 2026 HearUs Summit: Afghan Women’s Leadership in Achieving Justice and Peace through Accountability, 23 November 2026, Madrid
original_payload.original_body:
Afghanistan
Keynote remarks of SRSG Patten at the 2026 HearUs Summit: Afghan Women’s Leadership in Achieving Justice and Peace through Accountability, 23 November 2026, Madrid
Format
News and Press Release
Source
OSRSG Sexual Violence in Conflict
Posted
23 Nov 2026
Originally published
23 Nov 2026
Origin
View original
Excellencies, distinguished Ministers, representatives of Afghan women’s organizations, civil society leaders,
I would like to express my sincere gratitude to the Government of Spain for convening this important Summit and for its steadfast commitment to advancing the rights, participation and leadership of Afghan women and girls. I would also like to thank the Spanish authorities for their consistent support to my mandate and for their continued engagement in promoting justice and accountability. I also want to recognize the Afghan women who are here with us despite enormous risks: those working inside Afghanistan, as well as those forced to exile. I commend your extraordinary courage, resilience and leadership.
Five years since the Taliban seized power by force in August 2021, Afghanistan has become the world’s most devastating example of the systematic persecution of women and girls. No other country has imposed such extensive restrictions on half of its population solely on the basis of gender.
What began as a series of individual prohibitions against Afghan women and girls has evolved into an integrated legal and administrative framework designed to erase women from public life and institutionalize their subordination as a matter of state policy that now defines Taliban rule. Central to this ideology is the transformation of the justice system- from an institution that protects rights into one that enforces ideological conformity. From the perspective of my mandate, needless to say that, in the face of collapsed protection mechanisms, survivors have very limited opportunities to safely report incidents of conflict-related sexual violence. The dismantling of laws, institutions and courts has further eroded access to justice, leaving survivors with nowhere to turn for redress. Nonetheless, in the latest report of the Secretary-General, the UN verified incidents of rape, gang rape, forced marriage and other forms of sexual violence perpetrated against women and girls, including by de facto security forces.
Excellencies,
As of June 2026, the Taliban have issued 264 decrees affecting human rights, including 166 that specifically target the rights of Afghan women and girls. With every new decree, the space in which women and girls can learn, work, travel, make decisions, speak freely, or simply exist as independent human beings, has been further diminished. But the Taliban’s institutionalized misogyny extends beyond restricting women; it seeks to eliminate their visibility, autonomy, and agency. As a result, nearly 20 million Afghan women and girls live under a system intentionally designed to deny their agency and humanity. While Courts and state institutions no longer function as guarantors of justice, Afghan women continue to show us what it means to keep working for justice in the face of fear. They continue to lead from the front, documenting violations, preserving evidence, supporting survivors, mobilizing communities, and raising their voices before regional and international fora. It is critical for the international community to recognize the gravity of these crimes, crimes which may amount to a crime against humanity. These violations must be challenged, documented and accountability pursued.
Excellencies,
The situation in Afghanistan is much more than a human rights crisis; it is an accountability imperative for the international community. We cannot promise justice while allowing evidence, institutions and survivors’ support to disappear. Serious crimes cannot be treated as private matters, dismissed as inevitable or allowed to disappear with the passage of time. Accountability is not revenge. It is a refusal to accept that power places anyone above the law. It tells survivors that what happened to them matters. It helps prevent future crimes by making clear that perpetrators may be held accountable. No Afghan woman should be asked to wait for justice until it is politically convenient.
States should strengthen safe pathways to justice, support independent investigations and evidence collection and preservation especially at a time when some important international accountability avenues are shaping up for Afghanistan. While prospects for achieving justice in Taliban controlled Afghanistan are virtually non-existent and that the only avenues lie in international forums, there are some encouraging developments which I would like to highlight. Across international investigative mechanisms, international criminal justice, and State responsibility processes, the international community is demonstrating a growing determination to ensure that violations against women and girls are not met with impunity.
Firstly, there is the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan, established by the Human Rights Council in October 2025, mandated to “collect, consolidate, preserve and analyze evidence of international crimes and the most serious violations of international law committed in Afghanistan, and prepare files to facilitate and expedite fair and independent criminal proceedings”.
While the mechanism is a unique criminal justice body that can support international and national courts, including through universal jurisdiction, as well as proceedings before the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice and even a transitional justice process in Afghanistan itself, it is a matter of grave concern that due to the UN financial crisis, the Mechanism’s resourcing is in peril with cuts to critical posts that make it safe for survivors to come forward. From an already slimmed-down Mechanism, further cuts could leave it below the minimum it needs to deliver its mandate.
Excellencies,
The cost in lost evidence and survivors who never come forward, cannot be recovered later. The credibility and effectiveness of this critical mechanism will ultimately depend on whether it is provided with the resources necessary to carry out its work. Without adequate financial support, investigative capacity, witness protection measures and survivor-centered expertise, a critical opportunity to preserve evidence, advance accountability and lay the foundations for future justice risks being undermined at the very moment when it is most needed.
Yet, we have already witnessed the transformative potential of such mechanisms. In Myanmar, the Independent Investigative Mechanism contributed to the proceedings concerning State responsibility for genocide against the Rohingya. Last Thursday’s judgment by the International Court of Justice, which found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, including for sexual violence, represents a landmark step toward accountability and redress for one of the gravest crimes under international law. Importantly, the ICJ judgement recognized that the detailed witness statements collected by the Investigative Mechanism carried significant evidentiary weight, in light of the Mechanism’s careful methodology for gathering and analyzing evidence. This demonstrates a fundamental truth: rigorous documentation today lays the groundwork for justice tomorrow. In addition, the Mechanisms for both  Syria  and  Myanmar  show that it works even when those responsible remain in power and there is no access to the country.
The second important development is the International Criminal Court with the warrants of arrest issued by the Office of the Prosecutor in July and September 2025, for the crime against humanity of persecution on gender and on political grounds which were unsealed by the Pre-Trial Chamber on 5 October. These arrest warrants are a vindication of the rights of Afghan women and girls and demonstrate the OPT’s unwavering commitment to pursue accountability for gender-based crimes, including gender persecution.
Another important initiative is that launched in September 2024, by a group of member states, to hold the Taliban accountable for systemic violations of women’s and girls’ rights, invoking Article 29 – the dispute-settlement provision of the CEDAW Convention. While this initiative represents an important opportunity to affirm that systematic violations of women’s and girls’ rights carry consequences under international law, unfortunately two years into the process, there is no visible indication that negotiations are moving the dispute toward resolution. Instead, the Taliban have continued to expand and institutionalize restrictions on women and girls, with no meaningful signs of reversal or improvement. As negotiations appear stalled while violations deepen, the case for moving to the next procedural step is increasingly clear and urgent. Afghan women are calling on the coalition of governments to proceed to formal arbitration under Article 29. Doing so would undoubtedly sustain the momentum and credibility of this historic initiative.
Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen,
All these legal pathways are important frameworks for accountability. There is a unique opportunity with evidence preservation, individual criminal responsibility and State responsibility advancing in parallel. Collectively, these efforts send a clear message: the systematic oppression of women and girls is neither a domestic matter nor a political inevitability. It is a violation of international law that demands accountability, justice and redress.
The challenge before us now is to ensure that this accountability architecture is allowed to succeed. It requires political will, sustained commitment and resources. At the same time, we must ensure that Afghan women remain at the center of every effort. They are not only victims of these violations. They are leaders in the pursuit of accountability, documenting abuses, preserving evidence, supporting communities and keeping hope alive in the face of extraordinary adversity.
In conclusion, my message to Afghan women leaders and survivors is that their leadership deserves more than recognition; it deserves protection, resources and a genuine place in decisions. Their voices are essential to accountability, and their participation is essential to peace.
To member states and donors, I say – Afghan women continue to show us what it means to keep working for justice in the face of fear. The question before us is whether we will show the same determination in standing with them. Our commitments require consistency. We cannot praise women’s courage while leaving them without protection or resources. And we cannot promise justice while allowing evidence, institutions and survivor support to disappear.
The words “Hear Us” should not end when this Summit ends. They must be heard in funding decisions, diplomatic engagement, investigations and peace processes. They must be answered with protection, resources and action.
Let us therefore match that determination with action, by ensuring that the promises made do not remain words on paper, and by reaffirming that the fundamental rights of Afghan women and girls are not negotiable, not expendable, and not forgotten.
Thank you.

Summary of the Situation
Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 45 of 2026 (which ended on 14 November 2026), the Region of the Americas reported 58,795 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories, representing a 4.7-fold increase compared with the same period in 2025. Guatemala (34,860), Mexico (14,087), the United States (5,412), Peru (2,985), and Canada (1,128) account for the vast majority (99.5%) of confirmed cases (Map 1). A total of 84 deaths has been reported, including 53 in Guatemala, 23 in Mexico, six in the United States of America, one in Peru and one in Bolivia (1).
During EW 43 and EW 44 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 527 new confirmed cases of measles in seven countries and territories (Figure 1). Of the 527 new confirmed cases reported during EW 43–44, the United States accounted for 390, followed by Guatemala 73, Peru with 48, Mexico with nine, Belize with four, Canada with two, and Bolivia with one.
The 10–13 November meeting of the Regional Commission for the Monitoring and Re-Verification of Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination (RVC) reviewed the epidemiological situation of measles across the Region. Based on the Commission’s assessment and recommendations, which were subsequently endorsed by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Director, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, endemic measles transmission was determined to have been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico, and the United States, resulting in the loss of measles elimination status in all three countries.

items.title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police

original_payload.original_title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
original_payload.original_body:
Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
Image source,  Family handout
Image caption,    Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student
By   Nomsa Maseko   ,      Thuthuka Zondi      and    Eleanor Smallwood    ,  BBC World Service   ,   Reporting from Ekurhuleni
Published
2 hours ago
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.
Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.
After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."
Image source,  Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Image caption,    Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among  581 women who were killed in the country between July and September , according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.
There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women
Watch on iPlayer
Viewers outside the UK can watch on YouTube
In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."
He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.
The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.
Image source,  Reuters
Image caption,    The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."
Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.
Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".
Image source,  Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Image caption,    Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.
Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.
Image source,  Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Image caption,    Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.
She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.
When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.
"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.
Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.
She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.
Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.
In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.
She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.
Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.
Image source,  Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Image caption,    Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles
In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" -  after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.
She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body  was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later .
It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.
Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
Published
19 September
The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
Published
3 October
Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.
Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.
"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.
Image source,  Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Image caption,    Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed
Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.
Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.
Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.
Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."
This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe
Related topics
Femicide
Violence against women
South Africa

items.title:
Defense Procurement Reform in Africa: Lessons from Ukraine
  Ukraine’s wartime procurement innovations show that African governments can improve military effectiveness by adopting capability-based, tr

original_payload.original_title:
Defense Procurement Reform in Africa: Lessons from Ukraine
  Ukraine’s wartime procurement innovations show that African governments can improve military effectiveness by adopting capability-based, transparent, and domestically sourced procurement processes.
original_payload.original_body:
By  Joel Amegboh
November 23, 2026
Ukraine’s wartime procurement innovations show that African governments can improve military effectiveness by adopting capability-based, transparent, and domestically sourced procurement processes.
Radar and automatic identification system (AIS) in Madagascar enable operators to monitor the nautical and tactical situation of the marine environment in the region. (Photo:  Themys )
With its expansive territory and 1.5 billion people, Africa’s security landscape is characterized by great diversity and complexity. Violent extremist groups are spreading across the Sahel, with Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger accounting for over 40 percent of the nearly  24,000 annual terrorism-related deaths in Africa . Similar threats persist in the Lake Chad Basin, Somalia, and northern Mozambique. The escalating speed with which these violent extremist actors can access and deploy new technology, including  weaponized drones , is reshaping Africa’s security environment.
Africa also plays an increasingly critical role  in the international security architecture. Threats to African maritime shipping lanes, including the Bab al Mandab Strait connecting the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean, have strained international supply chains. The continent, similarly, faces a host of transnational threats including  organized crime , cyberattacks, and arms trafficking that imperil government authority and regional stability.
Security threats evolve faster than traditional acquisition cycles.
Responding effectively to this diverse and evolving threat environment requires African armed forces that are agile, technologically enabled, and adaptable to rapidly changing operational demands. Yet, Africa’s procurement systems are often misaligned to generate the weapons, logistical, and communications systems needed to defeat these evolving and often irregular security threats. Slow procurement processes, moreover, inhibit the rapid resupply of forces and equipment maintenance needed to sustain pressure on these threat actors.
These procurement challenges are reinforced by persistent fiscal pressures. Many African governments are often grappling with high public debt, limited domestic revenue, sluggish economic growth, inflation, currency depreciation, and recurring external shocks. These constraints significantly limit fiscal space for defense modernization. Consequently, many armed forces continue to operate with aging equipment, fragmented logistics systems, inadequate maintenance capacity, and heavy reliance on imported defense equipment.
These converging trends shape the parameters for defense planning across the continent. Substantially increasing defense budgets is neither fiscally sustainable nor politically feasible for many African governments. A central challenge, therefore, is how to achieve greater military capability within a highly constrained resource environment. Strengthening defense procurement is central to addressing this challenge and is a strategic imperative to improve military readiness, enhance resilience, and maximize the return on limited defense resources.
African Procurement Models are Under Pressure
Defense procurement has traditionally been viewed as an administrative function focused on acquiring military equipment. Moreover, procurement approaches for many African governments prioritize the acquisition of high-value conventional platforms like fighter aircraft, armored vehicles, naval vessels, and heavy weapon systems. Nigeria’s ongoing acquisition of  12 AH-1Z attack helicopters  and related equipment, for example, is valued at approximately $997 million.
Sustainment costs for big-ticket capital acquisitions compete directly with investments in intelligence, surveillance, mobility, logistics, cyber defense, and force readiness.
This pattern reflects broader regional trends. In West Africa,  arms imports doubled between 2015–2019 and 2020–2024 . Big-ticket items constitute a significant share of these limited defense budgets. In Ghana, illustratively, 30 percent of the $926 million defense allocation for 2026 was designated for  Air Force retooling and armored personnel carriers . In Nigeria, three-fourths of a $1.8 billion supplementary military budget approved in 2021 was  directed toward capital expenditure , including combat aircraft and offshore patrol vessels.
Such capital acquisitions create substantial long-term obligations for maintenance, spare parts, ammunition, infrastructure, software upgrades, and specialized training. These sustainment costs compete directly with investments in intelligence, surveillance, mobility, logistics, cyber defense, and force readiness, which, in many African countries, are more relevant to addressing contemporary security challenges.
Most African countries depend on external partners for the acquisition, maintenance, and modernization of military equipment, which can further compound these pressures. In addition to the higher costs frequently required, relying on foreign suppliers exposes procurement systems to exchange-rate volatility, supply-chain disruptions, export controls, delivery delays, and geopolitical uncertainty. The ongoing reliance on these external supply chains also limits opportunities for technology transfer, local manufacturing, and the development of domestic maintenance and repair capabilities.
A demonstration of a BlueBird Aerosystems Spylite Mini-UAS in service with the Senegalese military.
Sustaining imported equipment often proves as significant a financial challenge as acquiring it. In South Africa, shortages of spare parts, lengthy procurement lead times, funding constraints, and maintenance backlogs have  reduced the availability of critical military equipment . Some military helicopters have been in deep-level maintenance for more than 4 years, while inadequate funding for spare parts acquisition have  delayed the delivery of aircraft components  and their return to service. The strategic procurement challenge, therefore, is not just about procuring assets but ensuring that defense establishments have the financial, technical, and institutional capacity to sustain acquired capabilities throughout their operational life.
Persistent fiscal constraints further complicate procurement decisions. In many African countries,  personnel costs account for more than 60 percent of defense spending , leaving little funding for capital investment, research and development, maintenance, or capability enhancement.
Institutional weaknesses also undermine the effectiveness of defense procurement. Insufficiently professional and empowered procurement bodies are more prone to political pressures to pursue prestige projects that may contribute little to advancing national security priorities. Fragmented planning, weak acquisition management institutions, insufficient life-cycle cost analysis, limited contract oversight, and inadequate integration among procurement, logistics, and force planning, moreover, frequently reduce the return on defense investment. Procurement systems often prioritize equipment acquisition without adequately considering interoperability and infrastructure requirements. These shortcomings can lead to capability gaps, reduced equipment availability, and higher ownership costs over time.
A Nigerian Air Force helicopter is parked on the tarmac of the Maiduguri Air Force Base. (Photo: AFP)
In Botswana, illustratively, constrained acquisition budgets have led to the purchase of less expensive, older aircraft. However, these  require higher sustainment costs , which are becoming harder to source. Of three C-130Bs acquired by Botswana, one was eventually placed in storage and another was grounded in 2024, leaving only one of the original three in active service. Botswana subsequently received a C-130H  valued at approximately $30 million  and a package of 12,000 spare parts worth nearly $1 million. While donated, the experience shows how seemingly affordable acquisition decisions can generate substantial downstream costs if life-cycle requirements are not adequately anticipated and resourced.
The Evolution of Ukraine’s Agile Defense Procurement Process
Ukraine’s defense procurement system has undergone one of the most significant transformations in Europe in recent decades. Following independence in 1991, Ukraine inherited a large Soviet-era defense industrial base and a procurement system that was highly centralized, bureaucratic, and dominated by state-owned enterprises. Although the country possessed considerable manufacturing capacity, decades of underinvestment, fragmented governance, corruption, and weak institutional oversight limited its ability to modernize its armed forces efficiently. Procurement was often slow, opaque, and poorly coordinated. Limited investment in research, innovation, and industrial competitiveness reduced the sector’s responsiveness to evolving security threats.
These weaknesses were exposed in 2014 when Russia annexed parts of eastern Ukraine. Ukraine’s outdated procurement institutions could not rapidly equip military forces or sustain prolonged operations. This began a process of Ukraine fundamentally restructuring its defense procurement architecture—a process that was accelerated after Russia’s full-scale attack on Ukraine in 2022. The aims of the reforms were to improve transparency, speed, accountability, and operational effectiveness.
Ukraine’s experience demonstrates that defense procurement is not merely an administrative function but a strategic capability that directly influences military readiness, operational resilience, and national security.
The establishment of the Defense Procurement Agency (DPA) and the State Operator for Non-Lethal Acquisition (DOT) professionalized procurement management by separating weapons acquisition from logistics and sustainment. In practical terms, the reforms differentiated procurement policy and oversight from procurement execution. The Ministry of Defence retained responsibility for setting policy, defining requirements, allocating resources, and exercising oversight. Meanwhile, specialized agencies like the DOT assumed responsibility for contracting and supplier engagement. DPA was focused primarily on identifying the weapons, ammunition, and military equipment that Ukraine needed, while DOT managed food, clothing, fuel, and other non-lethal requirements.
This division clarified institutional responsibilities, reduced the Ministry’s direct involvement in individual procurement transactions, and allowed specialized acquisition organizations to develop dedicated contracting, market analysis, and supplier-management expertise. Direct contracting with manufacturers reduced reliance on intermediaries. As procurement regulations were progressively aligned with NATO standards, the adoption of international  best practices and oversight were prioritized .
Digital procurement systems increased transparency and accelerated contracting with manufacturers. By simplifying the weapons codification procedures and digitizing the process, redundancies were eliminated. The  codification timeline was reduced to 10 days , and manufacturers were able to submit and track their applications online. The effect was to significantly accelerate the timeline for bringing new weapons into military service.
At the same time, Ukraine expanded domestic defense production through the  Brave1 defense technology platform , which links government, industry, universities, and private innovators to rapidly develop drones, electronic warfare systems, robotics, and other emerging technologies. These reforms have enabled Ukraine to shorten procurement timelines, strengthen domestic production, improve accountability, and respond more rapidly to changing operational requirements.
Press conference of representatives of the Ministry of Defence and the Armed Forces of Ukraine. (Photo:  MDU )
The effects are  visible in the number of systems entering service . In 2023, the Ministry of Defence codified 405 models of weapons, including 244 produced domestically (46 percent of the total). The following year, more than 900 models were approved, with two-thirds allocated to Ukrainian manufacturers.
Specialized procurement agencies simultaneously expanded competition and strengthened financial discipline. During its first year, DOT concluded 719 contracts worth $1.6 billion—a  savings of $362 million . These changes created a shorter pathway from battlefield requirement to testing, codification, contracting, production, and fielding.
Ukraine’s experience demonstrates that defense procurement is not merely an administrative function but a strategic capability that directly influences military readiness, operational resilience, and national security. Countries that can rapidly acquire, produce, maintain, and adapt military capabilities are better positioned to respond to evolving threats, even when financial resources are constrained. Conversely, inefficient procurement institutions increase costs, delay modernization, and reduce military effectiveness regardless of the size of the defense budget.
For African governments, this lesson is especially important. They contend with persistent threats from terrorism, violent extremism, organized crime, piracy, cyberattacks, and border insecurity, all while operating under severe fiscal constraints. These conditions require procurement systems that maximize operational capability from limited resources rather than pursuing expensive, platform-centric modernization programs.
Practical Lessons from Ukraine’s Procurement Reforms
Ukraine’s reforms offer several practical lessons. First, procurement institutions should be modernized before procurement budgets are markedly expanded. Strengthening governance, professionalizing acquisition agencies, adopting digital procurement systems, and improving oversight can significantly improve the efficiency of existing defense spending without requiring substantial additional resources. During its first year, DOT realized substantial savings while its DOT-Chain digital system  accelerated the supply cycle fourfold .
Second, procurement should be driven by operational capability rather than prestige acquisitions. Investments in intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR), unmanned systems, secure communications, cyber defense, and logistics are often more relevant to Africa’s contemporary security environment than acquiring a limited number of expensive conventional platforms.
Procurement reform is a force multiplier.
Third, Ukraine shows that a robust domestic defense-industrial base is a strategic asset, not merely an economic objective. African governments should promote technology transfer, licensed production, public-private partnerships, and collaboration among defense institutions, universities, and local industry. Even where countries cannot manufacture complete weapon systems, building domestic capacity for maintenance, repair, ammunition production, software development, and unmanned technologies can reduce dependence on foreign suppliers, strengthen supply chain resilience, and create skilled jobs.
Finally, Ukraine illustrates that procurement resilience depends on institutional agility. Security threats evolve faster than traditional acquisition cycles. Procurement systems must therefore quickly incorporate new technologies, respond to changing operational requirements, and support continuous innovation.
A central lesson from Ukraine is that procurement reform is a force multiplier. By strengthening the efficiency of procurement institutions, investing in innovation, supporting domestic industry, and aligning acquisitions with operational requirements, African governments can achieve greater military effectiveness even with constrained defense budgets.
Click here for a printable PDF
Priorities for African Governments
The experience of Ukraine demonstrates that procurement reform, procurement agility, domestic defense industrial development, and rapid technological innovation can significantly enhance military readiness without a proportional increase in defense spending. For African governments, the challenge is therefore not simply to spend more on defense but to spend more strategically. As fiscal pressures continue to constrain military budgets, procurement systems must become more agile, accountable, and aligned with national security priorities.
Anchor procurement decisions in clearly defined national security strategies . Governments must make difficult choices about which capabilities are most urgent. By conducting threat assessments and integrating them into broader fiscal sustainability and debt management frameworks, governments are better able to prioritize strategically and integrate modernization requirements within available resources. In this way, they can balance investments in major platforms with operational requirements, including ISR, cyber defense, unmanned systems, communications, logistics, training, ammunition, and sustainment.
This requires a shift from reactive, platform-driven acquisitions to long-term capability development that is supported by multiyear budgeting that provides predictability for modernization programs while ensuring affordability. Procurement decisions should also incorporate life-cycle costs to ensure that new capabilities remain affordable and operational over time.
Countries that can rapidly acquire, produce, maintain, and adapt military capabilities are better positioned to respond to evolving threats, even when financial resources are constrained.
Strengthen procurement institutions . Establishing professional acquisition management, transparent oversight, and digital system institutions can improve efficiency and reduce delays. Strengthening the expertise of procurement personnel and contracting procedures enables translating strategic requirements into realistic capability specifications, assessing alternative systems, evaluating suppliers, negotiating contracts, and managing equipment throughout its life cycle.
These procurement organizations, in turn, need to be linked to operational commands, finance authorities, logistics organizations, and national security institutions to ensure that acquisition decisions reflect both operational requirements and available resources. Professionalizing procurement institutions can also help safeguard acquisition processes from political pressures for prestige purchases that may not align with the defined national security priorities.
Kenyan soldiers demonstrate the AeroVironment RQ-11 Raven micro-UAS.
Optimize domestic procurement . Defense procurement is part of a broader national resilience strategy rather than a stand-alone acquisition function. Developing domestic industrial capacity, expanding research and innovation partnerships, and strengthening maintenance and logistics systems can reduce reliance on external sources while improving operational readiness. For many African governments, broad defense industrial self-sufficiency may be neither financially sustainable nor operationally necessary, however, and should be approached selectively. Prioritization should be given to eliminating procurement dependencies that create unacceptable operational or strategic vulnerabilities.
Maintenance and repair, ammunition, selected spare parts, logistics support, technical training, and certain unmanned and dual-use technologies may offer attainable initial opportunities for developing local capacity. Sequencing procurement sourcing allows governments to build industrial and technical capacity over time while avoiding capability gaps that could result from attempting to replace established foreign supply chains too quickly. In some cases, technology transfer, licensed production, joint ventures, and local maintenance arrangements may provide a gradual pathway toward greater domestic capability.
Pursue strategic diversification . Acquiring systems from multiple international partners can provide governments with a more affordable and flexible solution to reducing dependence on a single supplier. Diversifying inventories can create additional requirements for training, maintenance, ammunition, spare parts, infrastructure, and technical support, however. Procurement decisions should therefore consider interoperability, fleet standardization, and sustainability alongside acquisition price and access to suppliers.
Expand regional cooperation . Joint procurement, shared maintenance facilities, standardized equipment, and collaborative industrial initiatives can increase purchasing leverage, improve interoperability, and strengthen collective security while easing the fiscal burden on individual countries. The African Union (AU) and regional economic communities (RECs) can provide frameworks for expanding cooperation in areas where individual national markets or defense budgets may be too limited to sustain capabilities independently. The  AU offers procurement principles  to which African defense procurement agencies can align their practices while progressively incorporating relevant international defense-specific standards for quality assurance and life-cycle management .  Regional approaches may be particularly valuable for specialized capabilities that are expensive to acquire and maintain but do not necessarily need to be replicated by every country.
Construct a regional defense industrial base . Rather than each country attempting to establish a comprehensive national defense industrial base, governments could identify areas of comparative advantage and develop complementary regional capabilities. One country may specialize in maintenance and repair, another in ammunition or selected components, and another in training, communications, or unmanned technologies. Such specialization could expand regional markets, improve economies of scale, and strengthen collective resilience while allowing governments to concentrate scarce resources in areas where they possess technological advantages.
Procurement Reform as a Strategic Capability
A robust domestic defense-industrial base is a strategic asset, not merely an economic objective.
Contemporary experience shows that procurement is a strategic capability that directly affects operational readiness, force sustainability, industrial resilience, technological innovation, and strategic autonomy. Transparent, adaptive, and professionally managed procurement systems can enable African governments to maximize limited financial resources into effective military capability.
A transition to capability-based procurement, supported by stronger governance, regional cooperation, and domestic industrial development, offers the most credible path to strengthening Africa’s defense readiness while preserving long-term fiscal sustainability.

items.title: In Focus: Critical Minerals

original_payload.original_title: In Focus: Critical Minerals
original_payload.original_body:
Africa’s vast reserves of critical minerals—including cobalt, lithium, graphite, copper, and rare earth elements—place the continent at the center of intensifying global competition for resources essential to advanced technologies, energy systems, and defense industries. This growing strategic importance presents opportunities and security challenges for African countries. External dominance of mineral supply chains, opaque mining agreements, environmental degradation, and competition over resource access risk reinforcing patterns of corruption, instability, and conflict. Yet, with stronger governance, diversified partnerships, and greater investment in domestic processing and infrastructure, African countries can leverage their mineral wealth to advance economic development, strengthen sovereignty, and promote long-term stability. The Africa Center’s analyses examine these evolving dynamics and the strategies African countries can pursue to ensure their critical minerals contribute to greater security and prosperity.
Spotlight
Transforming Africa’s Economic Corridors for a New Era
By Paul Nantulya
October 7, 2026
Africa’s regional economic corridors offer opportunities to strengthen integrated continental networks, but they require strong coordination bodies, diversified financing, and alignment with regional priorities.
Spotlight
Beyond M23: Addressing the Underlying Drivers of the DRC Conflict
By Paul Nantulya
July 29, 2026
Stabilizing eastern DRC will not ultimately be achieved on the battlefield, but by rebuilding intra-Congolese and African processes to address issues of citizenship, security sector reform, and greater transparency of the mineral sector.
Spotlight
Ghana’s Illegal Gold Mining Crisis: A National Security Threat with Regional Implications
By Edem Srem
July 21, 2026
The proliferation of “galamsey”—illicit gold mining and smuggling—has increasingly attracted criminal networks that rely on coercion and co-option to undermine security, the rule of law, and legitimate businesses.
Spotlight
Reciprocal and Resilient Mineral Supply Chains: Lessons from the Nacala Corridor
By Paul Nantulya
April 13, 2026
The Nacala Corridor illustrates how integrated mineral ecosystems can diversify access to strategic resources while enabling African value addition, accountability, and stability.
Spotlight
Chinese State-Owned Enterprises and Market Capture in Africa
By Paul Nantulya
March 17, 2026
Chinese SOEs serve as tools of national power—securing minerals, building alternative corridors to China’s economy, and shaping long-term influence—with far-reaching implications for African citizen interests and development.
Spotlight
China’s Critical Minerals Strategy in Africa
By Paul Nantulya*
December 9, 2025
China has gained a dominant position in Africa’s critical minerals sector through long-term investments in mining and refining capacity—factors that make it challenging for African countries to advance up the value chain.
Spotlight
Assessing Progress on Africa’s Agenda 2063
November 24, 2025
The African Union’s ambitious vision of citizen-focused development, infrastructural and institutional innovation, and sustained peace and security provides a template to harmonize intra- and interregional strategies.
Spotlight
Japan Innovates to Deepen Africa Relations
By Paul Nantulya
September 3, 2025
Japan’s TICAD process is strengthening Africa-Japan partnerships across economic, security, and development initiatives that rely on blended public-private financing and shared objectives.
Spotlight
The Limits to China’s Transactional Diplomacy in Africa
By Paul Nantulya
June 30, 2025
China’s regime agnostic diplomacy in Africa—investing in countries irrespective of a government’s adherence to the rule of law—holds inherent risks for Chinese investments and regional stability.
Spotlight
Africa’s Critical Minerals at a Critical Juncture
May 20, 2025
To benefit from the latest surge in global demand for strategic minerals, African countries must learn from past experiences and build transparent processes that advance stability and benefit ordinary citizens.

items.title: Africa: In Tokyo, Dr Sidi Ould Tah Calls On Japanese Companies to Invest More in Local Value Addition to African Resources

original_payload.original_title: Africa: In Tokyo, Dr Sidi Ould Tah Calls On Japanese Companies to Invest More in Local Value Addition to African Resources
original_payload.original_body:
African Development Bank Group President Dr Sidi Ould Tah has called on Japanese companies to invest more in the local processing and beneficiation of African resources, assuring that the Bank Group is ready to mobilise financing and risk-sharing instruments to support these investments.
He was speaking at a business roundtable organised by the Bank Group in collaboration with the Japanese private sector in Tokyo on 12 November, during his second official visit to Japan as President.
Dr Ould Tah outlined three investment priorities: promoting Africa's natural resources and creating greater value on the continent; developing the energy, transport and digital infrastructure essential for industrialisation; and harnessing Japanese technology and finance to support African businesses and bankable projects on the continent.
Addressing a large gathering of Japanese business leaders and representatives of private financial institutions and development finance institutions (DFIs),  Dr Ould Tah  said,
"Africa has the resources, markets and talent needed to become a major production hub. But this future will not be built solely on the export of raw materials." He invited them to forge a new generation of investment partnerships to transform African resources into added value, jobs and competitive industries.
Mr  Atsushi Mimura, Vice-Minister of Finance for International Affairs at the Japanese Ministry of Finance , said,
"The Ministry of Finance of Japan works closely with the African Development Bank to advance Africa's development priorities. With its deep knowledge of local markets and strong relationships across the continent, the Bank is a trusted partner for Japanese companies looking to develop or expand their operations in Africa."
President Ould Tah said Japan brings a powerful combination of engineering expertise, patient capital, cutting-edge technology and sound financial institutions. The Bank Group's strength, he added, lies in turning investment opportunities into viable operations through financing, guarantees, project preparation, policy dialogue and risk-mitigation instruments.

items.title: RDC: pourquoi les tensions s'accentuent entre l'Église catholique et le pouvoir

original_payload.original_title: RDC: pourquoi les tensions s'accentuent entre l'Église catholique et le pouvoir
original_payload.original_body:
RDC: pourquoi les tensions s'accentuent entre l'Église catholique et le pouvoir
En République démocratique du Congo (RDC), deux incidents ont opposé, en l'espace de deux jours, les forces de l'ordre aux responsables de l'Église catholique. Dimanche 22 novembre à Kinshasa, le cardinal Fridolin Ambongo a été contraint de délocaliser une messe. Le lendemain, à Lubumbashi, la police a dispersé une manifestation de l'Église. Deux événements qui interviennent dans un contexte de relations tendues entre les deux institutions, comme l’explique le politique Christian Moleka.

2 min     Temps de lecture
Écouter - 00:57
La cathédrale Saint-Pierre-et-Paul de Lubumbashi, le 4 décembre 2011. (Image d'illustration)         © Flickr.com CC BY-NC-SA 2.0 Fairphone
Par :
RFI
Publicité
À Kinshasa, dimanche, les forces de l'ordre ont empêché la célébration d'une messe du   cardinal Fridolin Ambongo  , qui devait s'adresser aux jeunes de son archidiocèse au stade Tata Raphaël.
Le lendemain, à Lubumbashi, dans le sud-est de la   RDC  , la police a dispersé à coups de gaz lacrymogènes une manifestation d'évêques et de fidèles qui réclamaient l'exécution d'un jugement en faveur de l'Église dans un dossier de spoliation foncière. Mgr Fulgence Muteba, archevêque de Lubumbashi et président de la Conférence épiscopale nationale du Congo (Cenco), devait prendre la tête du cortège.
Deux figures de l'Église en «  froid avec le régime  »
«  Ces incidents sont révélateurs de la tension latente entre l'Église catholique et le pouvoir de Kinshasa, mais particulièrement entre les personnalités du cardinal Ambongo et de Monseigneur Muteba, que Kinshasa considère comme plus ou moins radicaux  », explique l'analyste politique Christian Moleka au micro de notre   correspondante à Kinshasa,  Paulina Zidi .
Les deux hommes sont connus pour leurs prises de position critiques à l'égard du pouvoir congolais. «  Vous avez donc l'archevêque de Kinshasa qui, dans ses prises de position, est plus ou moins incisif vis-à-vis du régime  », poursuit Christian Moleka, qui rappelle que Mgr Muteba, à la tête de la Cenco,«  est également considéré comme quelqu'un de plus ou moins opposé dans sa dans sa prise de parole  ».
«  Et donc, ces deux événements ont pour lien des personnalités qui, plus ou moins, sont en froid avec le régime et qui ne sont pas connues pour leur capacité à avoir la langue dans leur poche  », poursuit Christian Moleka.
Le tout, «  dans un contexte où, depuis quelque temps, le pouvoir tente de créer des passerelles  » avec l'Église, notamment par une «  diplomatie de couloir  » qui «  n'aboutit pas  ». Ces incidents pourraient ainsi être révélateurs «  d'une forme d'agacement  » du pouvoir, voire constituer des moyens de pression «  que le pouvoir pourrait exercer sur les deux personnalités  ».

items.title: Nigeria: après les représailles meurtrières contre les Peuls, un appel à cesser les amalgames

original_payload.original_title: Nigeria: après les représailles meurtrières contre les Peuls, un appel à cesser les amalgames
original_payload.original_body:
Nigeria: après les représailles meurtrières contre les Peuls, un appel à cesser les amalgames
Dans le centre du Nigeria, au moins 64 Peuls ont été massacrés au cours du week-end dans l'État de Niger, en représailles à une attaque visant le village de Luman Ba'are, dont les habitants appartiennent en majorité à l'ethnie kambari. Après cette attaque meurtrière, les membres des milices d'autodéfense locales s'en sont pris à des campements habités par des éleveurs peuls dans plusieurs villages du district de Borgu.
Mettre RFI en favori sur Google
pour voir les contenus de RFI s’afficher en priorité dans vos résultats de recherche.
Publié le :  24/11/2026 - 06:08
1 min     Temps de lecture
Localisation de Wawa, au Nigeria.        © RFI
Par :
RFI avec AFP
Publicité
Au   Nigeria  , des hommes armés ont incendié des maisons, volé du bétail et tué plusieurs habitants de Luman Ba'are, dont le chef du village, sa femme et ses trois enfants. Selon les habitants de Luman Ba'are, les assaillants étaient des Peuls. Les groupes d'autodéfense locaux ont alors pris pour cible des communautés peules, notamment à Wawa et Gadi Oli.
Les miliciens ont pillé les campements et mutilé des Peuls innocents, selon le Dr Salim Musa Umar, représentant de l'organisation Fulbe Global Development and Right Initiatives.
«  Ces bandits ou ces jihadistes ne représentent en rien la communauté peule. Il faut mettre fin à ces généralisations. Les auteurs de ces actes odieux doivent être identifiés. Cela permettra d'éviter des représailles et de dissuader d'autres groupes d'autodéfense de semer le chaos sans raison. La communauté peule qui a été prise pour cible vit paisiblement et subit elle aussi les atrocités perpétrées par ces groupes armés  », explique-t-il au micro de notre journaliste du service Afrique,  Liza Fabbian .
Les victimes de cette tuerie, qui a visé indistinctement femmes, enfants et vieillards, ont été inhumées au cours du week-end. D'autres victimes ont été transportées à l'hôpital, alors que plusieurs membres de ces communautés à majorité peule sont toujours portés disparus.
Les miliciens s'en sont également pris au bétail, qui constitue souvent le seul moyen de subsistance de ces familles peules.

items.title: Madagascar: mandats d'arrêt requis contre l'ancien président Rajoelina et son ex-Premier ministre dans l'affaire Boeing

original_payload.original_title: Madagascar: mandats d'arrêt requis contre l'ancien président Rajoelina et son ex-Premier ministre dans l'affaire Boeing
original_payload.original_body:
Madagascar: mandats d'arrêt requis contre l'ancien président Rajoelina et son ex-Premier ministre dans l'affaire Boeing
À Madagascar, l'ancien président Andry Rajoelina est rattrapé par l'affaire des Boeing envoyés en Iran. Le parquet anticorruption demande la délivrance de mandats d'arrêt contre lui et son ancien Premier ministre, Christian Ntsay, notamment pour financement du terrorisme. Les deux hommes ont fui le pays en octobre 2025.

Avec notre correspondante à Antananarivo,   Aurélie Kouman
En juillet 2025, c'est   Andry Rajoelina   lui-même qui annonce les premières arrestations. Cinq Boeing 777, immatriculés provisoirement à   Madagascar  , viennent d'être retrouvés en   Iran  .
Son Premier ministre, Christian Ntsay, assure alors que ni lui ni le président n'étaient informés. Seize mois plus tard, les deux hommes, chassés du pouvoir entre-temps, sont poursuivis pour financement du terrorisme. Le parquet demande leur arrestation.
À lire aussi  Ouverture du procès de l'affaire des «Boeings iraniens» immatriculés à Madagascar
Deux dossiers judiciaires
L'affaire compte désormais deux dossiers. Le premier porte sur l'opération elle-même : l'immatriculation des avions et leur envoi illégal vers l'Iran. Il vise 32 prévenus malgaches, iraniens et indiens. Jugé début novembre, ce dossier sera examiné en appel le 27 novembre.
Le second est né d'une nouvelle plainte de l'Aviation civile, en octobre. Il vise ces mêmes 32 prévenus et en ajoute treize, dont l'ancien président et son Premier ministre. Il est cette fois question de financement du terrorisme et de fourniture d'armes de guerre. Selon le parquet, la compagnie iranienne qui a récupéré les avions fait en effet partie d'un réseau terroriste.
Onze suspects sont en détention provisoire. Les mandats d'arrêt doivent encore être délivrés par un juge.

items.title: Sénégal: les boulangers en grève pour réclamer une hausse du prix du pain

original_payload.original_title: Sénégal: les boulangers en grève pour réclamer une hausse du prix du pain
original_payload.original_body:
Sénégal: les boulangers en grève pour réclamer une hausse du prix du pain
Au Sénégal, ce mardi 24 novembre marque le deuxième jour de la grève du pain, prévue jusqu'à mercredi inclus. Les boulangers du pays ont été appelés à arrêter leur production par trois des quatre syndicats patronaux du secteur. Selon ces derniers, 35 % des boulangeries ont fermé leurs portes lundi en moyenne à travers le pays, un taux qui avoisine les 40 % dans la région de Dakar. Les professionnels dénoncent une explosion de leurs charges et réclament l'augmentation du prix de la baguette de 190 grammes, fixé par l'État.

2 min     Temps de lecture
Écouter - 01:19
Des baguettes sont exposées sur le comptoir d'une épicerie du quartier de Sicap, à Dakar, le 18 mars 2020.        AFP - SEYLLOU
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondante à Dakar,   Pauline Le Troquier
Dans les rues de Dakar, certains habitants ont trouvé lundi les rideaux de leurs boulangeries habituelles fermés. Les professionnels du secteur dénoncent une explosion des charges à supporter, notamment du prix de la farine et de l'électricité. Même si, dans cette boulangerie de la Cité Keur Gorgui, les fours ont continué de tourner, son propriétaire décrit lui aussi une situation intenable.
«  La situation des boulangers au   Sénégal   est très difficile. En fait, on ne s'en sort pas. On ne gagne presque pas d'argent sur une baguette vendue et nos charges sont trop lourdes, la farine trop chère, l'électricité aussi. C'est plus possible.  »
À lire aussi  Sénégal: les boulangers exigent de l’État un prix plus élevé pour la baguette
Le gouvernement refuse d'augmenter le prix du pain
Dans un communiqué publié lundi, le ministre de l'Industrie et du Commerce a campé sur son refus d'augmenter le prix du pain, de 150 francs CFA (23 centimes d'euro) aujourd'hui à 210 francs CFA (32 centimes d'euro). C'est la principale revendication des syndicats. Une proposition «  inacceptable  », répondent les autorités, au vu d'un contexte économique déjà difficile pour les ménages.
Pour Souleymane Seck, membre de l'Intersyndicale de la boulangerie du Sénégal, à l'origine du mot d'ordre, le ministre n'a pas pris en considération les revendications des boulangers lors d'une rencontre organisée il y a dix jours avec les syndicats.
Il parle d'un produit social. C'est à l'État de financer le produit social, c'est pas aux boulangers. On n'a pas assez de marges bénéficiaires, là, pour pouvoir financer tout ça. Vous ne pouvez rien faire pour nous. OK, d'accord, on va, on va au clash. On le souhaite pas, hein ? Parce que vraiment, nous sommes tous les jours en face des populations. Néanmoins, les boulangers, on ne peut plus continuer comme ça. Pourquoi ? Parce qu'on perd de l'argent.
00:50
