items.title: NCC boss urges staff to strengthen institutional values

original_payload.original_title: NCC boss urges staff to strengthen institutional values
original_payload.original_body:
Entertainment  NCC boss urges staff to strengthen institutional values
By  Joshua Olomu   ·   43 minutes ago   ·  6 min read
✓
✓
By Priscilla Osaje
Dr John Asein, Director-General, Nigerian Copyright Commission (NCC), has called on the Management Staff and State Commandants of the commission to strengthen institutional values and agree on standards and priorities that would drive greater results.
Asein made the call at the opening of a four-day Strategic Retreat and Institutional Performance Review for management staff and state commandants of the commission, on Monday in Abuja.
The retreat was themed: “Consolidating the Grains of the NCC Transformation Agenda for a Future – Ready Copyright System in Nigeria”.
According to him, the retreat aimed to enable the commission take stock, challenge themselves and chart a stronger future.
According to him, the retreat is   more than a review of activities, but a forum for constructive peer assessment, inclusive policy formulation and collective ownership of our institutional goals.
He therefore urged to participants to use the opportunity that the retreat offers  to assess their performances
“We must be candid in admitting our shortcomings, generous in sharing our successes, and courageous in embracing change.
“Our task is to build a stronger, more united and effective commission, where every officer contributes. Excellence is the standard and performance is measured by impact,” he said.
Asein said that the objective of this retreat was to promote constructive peer review and institutional learning, where departments, units, and state commands would have the opportunity to examine one another’s performance and  exchange experiences.
He stressed that peer review must not become an exercise in fault-finding or assigning blame, but should encourage honest assessment, mutual respect and shared learning.
“Where a department or command has excelled, we should identify the factors responsible and explore how those lessons can be applied elsewhere.
“Where performance has fallen below expectations, we should understand the difficulties and agree on corrective measures.
“The purpose is not to determine who is better than others, but to help everyone become better at what they do because no office has a monopoly of good ideas.
“”No officer is too senior to learn, and none is too junior to make a useful contribution. We must build an institution that learns from its experiences, values constructive criticism and continuously improves its processes,” he advised.
Beyond reviewing performance, the NCC DG said the retreat must also help them define and strengthen the values that bind them together as an institution.
He said NCC is characterised by Integrity, discipline, professionalism, diligence, accountability, teamwork and commitment.
Asein described the retreat as the most important outcomes for establishing  a clearer standards for performance and service delivery.
He charged the staff to define what was expected of every department, unit, and state command to establish measurable targets and strengthen accountability for results.
“Our standards must reflect not only operational success, but also integrity, professionalism, initiative, responsiveness, teamwork and prudent management of resources.
“Performance must be assessed objectively; excellence must be recognised and rewarded in this connection.
” I am pleased to announce the introduction of the Director-General’s ‘Distinguished Command Trophy’, which will become a permanent feature of our annual recognition and reward programme,” he said.
According to the D-G, the maiden award will be presented at the retreat together with a substantial cash prize for the winning state command.
He said the award recognised all-round excellence, taking into account discipline, integrity, initiative, operational achievements, quality of reporting, among other criteria.
Speaking on the commission’s priorities going forward as they prepare for 2027, the NCC boss urged participants to focus on clear strategic priorities.
“We must consolidate the implementation of the Copyright Act, 2022, strengthen enforcement against piracy, particularly in the digital environment, and deepen cooperation with relevant institutions.
“We must modernise our regulatory and administrative processes, improve service delivery, strengthen the oversight of collective management organisations and promote greater transparency and accountability in copyright-related revenue administration,” he said.
He also called for increased investment in staff development, improve supervision, promotion of  innovation and strengthened  capacity to respond to emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence,” he said.
In his keynote address, Mr Olusegun Adekunle, said the retreat was aimed at producing an establishment  verified institutional baseline for 2019–2026,  where every major claimed achievement should be supported by evidence and classified as activity, output, outcome or impact.
Adekunle, former Permanent Secretary, General Services, Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), spoke on ‘Sustaining the New Copyright Narrative Through Strategic Management.
According to him, NCC should adapt an annual institutional scorecard, adding that the annual retreat should not become a ceremony, but it should answer several questions.
“Headquarters and state commands should operate through a  shared performance architecture. State commands should have common core indicators, but also contextual indicators reflecting workload, territory, resources and creative-industry concentration.
“A fair system should balance outcomes, professionalism, integrity, innovation, stakeholder engagement, reporting quality, efficient resource use and performance relative to opportunity,” he said.
He urged the commission to adopt a three-year institutional capability programme covering digital enforcement, AI policy, CMO oversight, data management, prosecution, economics and leadership succession.
Adekunle stressed that the commission should also create an implementation discipline, where every retreat resolution should have an owner, deadline, performance indicator, resource requirement and review date.
He further said that to ensure an  effective governance, the commission should increasingly operate through written systems rather than institutional memory residing in individuals.
He noted that the Copyright Act gives the commission broad functions covering administration, regulation, enforcement and advice to government on international copyright arrangements.
“Copyright policy should go beyond cultural issue, but connected with trade, digital policy, education, technology, broadcasting, investment, taxation, consumer protection and economic diversification.
“The commission should therefore cultivate durable relationships across government. Let me warn however that political support must never be allowed to become political dependence.
” A sustainable regulator like the NCC must be able to demonstrate its relevance through evidence, law, public value and professional competence,” he added
He urged NCC to move from training by opportunity and patronage to training based on a competency framework.
Lynda Alphaeus, Director and Commandant, Lagos command of the commission, said the retreat had been very impactful, adding that they would ensure they have plans at the end of the programme.
According to her, there must be plans for what they are going to deliver to ensure that   by 2027 they will be able to check progress made.
“That serves as a reminder that for every piece of work we do, there is still more work to be done.
“We must be effective, not just by having a good copyright act, but by enforcing it for the benefit of copyright owners,” she said.
Another participant, Mrs. Olufunmilayo Adewale, Director of the Nigerian Copyright Academy, said the programme was a steep learning curve for them, adding that what they had learned would help institutionalise knowledge.
“We also believe that by the time we meet again in 2027, NCC will have better stories to tell and will have delivered even more to the Nigerian public,” she said.(NAN)

items.title: Stakeholders seek payment reforms to improve power supply

original_payload.original_title: Stakeholders seek payment reforms to improve power supply
original_payload.original_body:
Economy/Business  Stakeholders seek payment reforms to improve power supply
By  Folashade Adeniran   ·   2 hours ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Joy Oyerinde
Energy stakeholders have identified weak payment arrangements and inadequate gas supply as major constraints to reliable electricity supply in Nigeria.
They ‌‍‌⁠ ⁠‍made the observation at a joint seminar organised in Lagos on Monday by the Power and Energy Sectoral Group, in collaboration with the Oil and Gas Sectoral Group of the Chartered Institute of Directors Nigeria (CIoD).
The seminar, with the theme: “X-raying the Interconnections Between the Power Sector Value Chain and Efficient Power Supply in Nigeria”,  examined challenges affecting gas supply, electricity generation, transmission and distribution.
Speaking at the seminar, Mr Olayemi Solar, Chief Executive Officer, Quad Gas and Power Ltd., said Nigeria’s vast gas reserves and installed generation capacity had not translated into adequate electricity supply because of commercial and operational gaps across the value chain.
Solar’s presentation showed that Nigeria had 215 trillion cubic feet of proven and probable gas reserves as at Jan. 1, and installed grid-connected generation capacity of 13,625 megawatts.
However, average grid generation stood at 4,089 megawatts in September.
He highlighted payment challenges within the electricity market, noting that Distribution Companies (DisCos) remitted N307 billion against gross generation invoices of N648 billion in the second quarter of the year.
The presentation showed that the amount represented 47 per cent of the gross invoices, although DisCos met 93.9 per cent of their adjusted remittance obligations.
Solar said the figures underscored the need for sustainable payment arrangements that would enable power generation companies (GenCos) to meet their obligations to gas suppliers and support continued investment in gas infrastructure.
He also highlighted the gap between domestic gas delivery obligations and actual supply, citing average delivery of 2.05 billion cubic feet per day against an obligation of 3.16 billion cubic feet per day in the first half of the year.
Solar called for better alignment of gas supply agreements, transportation agreements and power purchase agreements to ensure that payment obligations, delivery commitments and contractual risks were properly coordinated.
He also proposed the establishment of a Gas-to-Power Commercial Sustainability Working Group under CIoD to develop a reconciled industry-wide baseline, standard contractual terms and a funded payment-security mechanism for current invoices.
Earlier, Mr Fisayo Duduyemi, First Vice-President, Nigerian Gas Association, said Nigeria required an estimated 33 gigawatts of electricity generation capacity for reliable supply, while grid delivery frequently remained around four gigawatts.
Duduyemi, who is also Executive Vice-President, Integrated Power, Axxela Ltd., said the country’s electricity challenges had forced businesses to commit scarce resources to generators, fuel and maintenance rather than productive investments.
He identified gas availability, infrastructure constraints and market liquidity as major challenges affecting the gas-to-power chain.
According to him, inadequate gas supply reduces generation, while transmission limitations prevent available electricity from reaching consumers.
He said weak revenue collection and market payments also affected generators’ ability to settle obligations to gas suppliers.
“Energy must move from the wellhead to the customer, and money must move reliably back through the chain,” he said.
Duduyemi called for increased investment in gas development, interconnected pipeline infrastructure and transmission, alongside decentralised electricity solutions.
He said investors required regulatory certainty, commercially viable pricing and credible payment arrangements to commit funds to gas exploration, processing and transportation infrastructure.
Also speaking, Mr Yinka Adelodun, Chief Executive Officer, ADEOCAN Power Services Ltd., advocated greater investment in smart Internet of Things (IoT) metering to improve electricity distribution efficiency, revenue assurance and consumer confidence.
In his presentation, Adelodun said smart meters should be treated as essential digital grid infrastructure rather than merely tools for billing and revenue collection.
He explained that real-time metering data could help distribution companies monitor electricity consumption, identify overloaded transformers, detect abnormal consumption and improve network investment decisions.
In his welcome remarks, Prof. Felix Amieyeofori, Chairman, Power and Energy Sectoral Group, said the institute would use the outcome of the seminar to develop a Governance Advocacy Policy Document on key issues affecting the power and energy sectors.
He said the document would guide the institute’s engagements with regulators, policymakers, government institutions and other industry stakeholders.
Amieyeofori said stronger collaboration between the oil and gas and power sectors was necessary to address challenges affecting electricity generation and supply.
In his opening remarks, Chief Adetunji Oyebanji, President and Chairman of Council, said Nigeria’s ambition of building a one-trillion-dollar economy required a dependable and commercially viable energy sector.
Oyebanji, who said he had spent more than 46 years in the energy industry, stressed the need for effective institutions, infrastructure development, sound commercial arrangements and partnerships to translate the country’s natural resources into economic benefits.
He urged stakeholders to move beyond identifying challenges and develop practical recommendations to strengthen collaboration across the energy value chain.(NAN)

original_payload.original_title: Stockbroker projects improved market liquidity after Dangote Refinery IPO allotment
original_payload.original_body:
Economy/Business  Stockbroker projects improved market liquidity after Dangote Refinery IPO allotment
By  Folashade Adeniran   ·   2 hours ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Taiye Olayemi
A stockbroker, Mr David Adonri, has projected improved liquidity in the Nigerian equities market following the completion of the Dangote Refinery Initial Public Offering (IPO) allotment.
Adonri, Vice President of Highcap Securities Ltd., gave the projection in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Monday in Lagos.
He said the return of funds to unsuccessful applicants would release liquidity into the secondary market and potentially ease the ongoing bearish trend.
He spoke against the backdrop of Monday’s market performance, as investors lost N767 billion in market capitalisation, extending the market’s losses to five consecutive trading sessions.
He attributed the downturn to funds diverted from the secondary market into the Dangote Refinery IPO, creating liquidity constraints.
According to him, substantial funds that would ordinarily circulate in the secondary market are currently tied up in the primary market.
“Clearly, the market decline is as a result of a liquidity squeeze in the secondary market because funds that normally rotate within the market have been trapped in the primary market through the refinery IPO.
“By next week, when the allotment would have been made and monies returned for unsuccessful applications, more liquidity will come into the secondary market.
“The release of funds after the IPO allotment next week will support renewed trading activities in the secondary market,” he said.
Adonri explained that the current market situation was largely a temporary liquidity-driven downturn rather than a reflection of weaknesses in the underlying macroeconomic environment.
He noted that inflation had been moderating, the Naira remained relatively stable, while crude oil prices, in spite of a slight decline, remained above the benchmark used in the national budget.
He said political activities ahead of the 2027 general elections could also have been a possible factor influencing market sentiment.
Adonri, however, expressed reservations about attributing the downturn to election-related concerns as he noted that the market had experienced several election cycles.
He said the market should have developed sufficient resilience to withstand political uncertainties associated with election campaigns. (NAN)

items.title: Africa moves to leverage intellectual property for economic growth

original_payload.original_title: Africa moves to leverage intellectual property for economic growth
original_payload.original_body:
Economy/Business  Africa moves to leverage intellectual property for economic growth
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   2 hours ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Vivian Emoni
Mr Sand Mba-Kalu, Chaiman, All Africa Intellectual Property Summit (AAIPS), has called for stronger collaboration among governments, businesses and research institutions to maximise the continent’s economic benefits from innovation and creativity.
Mba-Kalu made the call while briefing newsmen on the outcome of the 7th AAIPS, on Monday in Abuja.
He said the essence of the briefing was also to announce the Nairobi Declaration on Intellectual Property and Africa’s Economic Transformation and the inuaguration of Governing Council of the All Africa Intellectual Property Association.
He said the adoption was to promote intellectual property as a driver of Africa’s economic transformation, adding that the inuaguration of the council was to strengthen continental cooperation on intellectual property.
“The seventh edition of the summit which held in Nairobi, Kenya, from Nov. 11 to Nov. 13, 2026, focused on mainstreaming intellectual property into Africa’s trade, industrial and creative economy transformation.
“The declaration provided a common direction for cooperation across trade, industry, research, health and the creative economy.
“Intellectual property is critical to determining how inventions, businesses’ brands and creative works generated economic value.
“Africa must earn greater value from the knowledge, inventions and creative works of its people,” he said.
The AAIPS organising committee chairman said the declaration would connect intellectual property protection and utilisation with economic growth and improved livelihoods across the continent.
He called for closer coordination among trade authorities, intellectual property institutions, export promotion agencies and business support organisations.
He said that African enterprises needed accessible information on intellectual property protection, costs, procedures, contracts and dispute resolution to compete effectively in regional and global markets.
He said intellectual property could support Africa’s pharmaceutical manufacturing ambitions through research collaboration, licensing and technology transfer.
Mba-Kalu emphasised the need to combine industrial development with investments in manufacturing capacity and effective regulation to ensure access to safe, affordable and quality medicines.
He also called for stronger partnerships among universities, research institutes and businesses to translate research discoveries into commercially useful products.
He said that researchers required support to assess market demand, establish ownership rights and develop agreements with partners capable of commercialising their inventions.
He urged financial institutions, investors and development partners to develop financing opportunities based on the commercial value of intellectual property assets.
According to him, clear ownership, sound contracts, market demand and realistic revenue projections could improve enterprises’ investment prospects.
On the creative economy, Mba-Kalu called for transparent royalty collection and payment systems to ensure musicians, filmmakers, writers, designers and performers received fair earnings.
He said African creators and technology businesses must participate in discussions on artificial intelligence, particularly concerning licensing, attribution and remuneration for creative works.
He also emphasised the need to extend intellectual property support to small businesses, women, young innovators and communities whose knowledge and cultural expressions contributed to Africa’s wealth.
Mba-Kalu said that cooperation involving traditional knowledge must respect affected communities, their participation in decisions and fair sharing of benefits.
He added that the inauguration of the association council would provide a platform for sustained professional cooperation among intellectual property institutions, practitioners, researchers and businesses across Africa.
According to him, the association will promote knowledge exchange, partnerships and continued engagement between editions of the summit.
The AAIPS chairman described research and publications as important tools for strengthening intellectual property policies and practices.
Mba-Kalu urged African governments to integrate intellectual property into industrial, trade and innovation policies, supported by capable institutions and accessible services.
He called on businesses, investors, universities and international partners to strengthen investment, research collaboration, technology transfer and market access.
He said that delegates had selected Botswana to host the eighth AAIP summit in 2027.
“The summit’s outcomes will be assessed through measurable improvements in research commercialisation, licensing agreements, production capacity, access to intellectual property services and business opportunities,” he said. (NAN)

original_payload.original_title: VP Shettima inaugurates innovation hub to boost digital skills, youth entrepreneurship
original_payload.original_body:
Science & Tech  VP Shettima inaugurates innovation hub to boost digital skills, youth entrepreneurship
By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   2 hours ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Ahmed Kaigama
Vice-President Kashim Shettima has inaugurated the Ambassador Babagana Kingibe Innovation Hub in Maiduguri to promote digital skills, innovation and entrepreneurship among youths in Borno and the North-East.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the hub is established through a partnership between the Federal Government, Borno and IHS Nigeria.
Shettima said the facility would provide young Nigerians with opportunities to develop their talents, transform innovative ideas into businesses and participate in the country’s growing digital economy.
The Vice-President said digital innovation remained critical to Nigeria’s economic transformation, stressing the need to extend technology-driven opportunities beyond major cities.
He described the hub as a platform for young people to acquire relevant skills, develop innovative solutions and explore opportunities in the technology ecosystem.
“What stands before us today is a playground of ideas for our young people,” he said.
Shettima commended IHS Nigeria for supporting the initiative, noting that public-private partnerships were essential to advancing national development.
He expressed hope that the facility would become a centre of excellence and a launchpad for young innovators to contribute to Nigeria’s technological and economic growth.
Also speaking, the Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Dr Bosun Tijani, said the hub would strengthen digital skills, innovation and business development in Borno and the wider North-East.
Tijani said the initiative was conceived about two years ago following discussions with the Borno Government on establishing a technology hub to provide opportunities for young people and entrepreneurs.
He said the facility was designed to replicate technology-driven activities available in major cities such as Lagos, thereby decentralising the country’s digital economy.
According to him, the hub will provide opportunities for digital learning, entrepreneurship, business development and innovation.
In his remarks, the Chief Executive Officer of IHS Nigeria, Mohamad Darwish, represented by the Deputy CEO, Kazeem Oladepo, said the facility was established to unlock the digital potential of youths across Borno and the North-East.
He said the hub would enable young people to acquire digital skills, access mentorship, develop startups, attract investment and create employment opportunities.
Darwish urged youths to utilise the facility to develop innovative solutions capable of addressing challenges in their communities.
He reaffirmed IHS Nigeria’s commitment to supporting education, entrepreneurship and digital inclusion across the country.
The facility is expected to serve as a centre for digital learning, innovation, mentorship and business development. (NAN)

items.title: 128 bag first-class as Igbinedion varsity graduates 1,204 students

original_payload.original_title: 128 bag first-class as Igbinedion varsity graduates 1,204 students
original_payload.original_body:
General News  128 bag first-class as Igbinedion varsity graduates 1,204 students
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   2 hours ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Usman Aliyu
Igbinedion University, Okada, Edo, says 128 graduands earned first-class degrees as the institution graduates 1,204 students at its 24th convocation.
Prof. Lawrence Ezemonye, Vice-Chancellor, disclosed this on Monday in Okada, Eso, during a news conference ahead of the convocation scheduled for Saturday.
He said the graduating class comprised 961 undergraduate students and 242 postgraduate, which included 54 Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D) holders, 167 master’s degree recipients and 22 postgraduate diploma graduates.
Of the undergraduate graduands, he said 425 made Second Class Upper, while 196 obtained Second Class Lower degrees.
According to him, a further 212 students will receive unclassified degrees in Medicine and Pharmacy.
Ezemonye said the number of graduands increased from 1,050 at the university’s 23rd convocation in November 2025.
“This growth is a positive reflection of the University’s expanding academic community and sustained commitment to student success,” he said.
He disclosed that the university recorded 15 distinctions in Community Medicine, five in Internal Medicine and five in Surgery.
In professional examinations, he said the institution recorded 100 per cent success in Medical Laboratory Science examinations in the last two years, alongside 81 per cent in General Nursing and 82 per cent in Midwifery, he said.
The convocation lecture, according to him, will be delivered by the Chairman of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA), Brig.-Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa (rtd.).
Ezemonye said the lecture would challenge graduates to look beyond certificates and embrace entrepreneurship, innovation and productive contributions to national development.
“Education must empower graduates not only to seek opportunities but also to create them,” he said.
The vice-chancellor announced that the National Universities Commission had approved new undergraduate and postgraduate programmes for the 2026/2027 academic session.
The undergraduate programmes, he said, were Bachelor of Science in Intelligence and Security Studies, Public Health, and Healthcare Administration and Hospital Management.
Ezemonye said that the postgraduate programmes included diplomas in Business Administration, Accounting, Banking and Finance, Political Science, Sociology, Microbiology and Biochemistry, as well as Master of Science and Ph.D in Anatomy.
“The introduction of these programmes reflects our determination to respond proactively to emerging national needs,” he said.
The vice-chancellor said the university currently offered 102 accredited academic programmes across 37 departments, seven colleges and three schools.
On research, he said the university had secured grants, including an European Union-funded project on sustainable plastic waste management and recycling involving Nigeria and South Africa.
He said the institution had also secured the SWARM2SCALE research grant to advance plastic recycling and circular economy initiatives.
The university, in partnership with Harvard University, he noted, had installed 10 PurpleAir air-quality monitoring sensors across its campus.
The sensors, he explained, would provide near-real-time data on particulate matter to support air pollution assessment, environmental research and evidence-based decision-making.
On infrastructure, Ezemonye said the university had procured two 1.5-megawatt gas-fired power plants for installation at Okokpon Village in Ovia South-West Local Government Area.
“The project is designed to improve energy security, reduce operating costs and provide more reliable electricity for teaching, research and healthcare services,” he said.
He added that 200 staff accommodation flats had been completed, while construction of student hostels, including facilities for medical and nursing students, was nearing completion.
He said the university would also intensify the integration of artificial intelligence and virtual reality into teaching and learning.
Ezemonye reaffirmed the university’s zero-tolerance policy on cultism, drug abuse, examination misconduct, bullying and cybercrime.
The vice-chancellor said the university, established in 1999 as Nigeria’s first licensed private university, had graduated more than 16,000 students, including over 3,000 medical doctors.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the convocation activities would continue with a play, The Altine’s Wrath, by Femi Osofisan, on Thursday, followed by a Juma’at service and alumni reunion on Friday.
The degree conferment and award of prizes would hold on Saturday, while a thanksgiving service was scheduled for Sunday.(NAN)

items.title: NAN, diction consultancy train staff on spoken English, communication skills

original_payload.original_title: NAN, diction consultancy train staff on spoken English, communication skills
original_payload.original_body:
General News  NAN, diction consultancy train staff on spoken English, communication skills
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   2 hours ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Linda Ogbonna/Kudirat Habeeb
The  News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) , in partnership with Vethans Diction Consultancy, on Monday trained its editorial staff to improve their diction of spoken English and communication skills.
The one-day training held in Lagos, focused on effective speech delivery, correct pronunciation, proper articulation of English sounds and the appropriate use of spoken English in professional communication.
Speaking during the training, the Principal Consultant, Vethans Diction Consultancy, Mrs Loveth Nimkur-Ikilama, said that it was designed to equip journalists with the skills needed to communicate clearly, confidently and effectively through speech.
Nimkur-Ikilama, who facilitated the training, identified mother tongue interference, poor learning environment and inadequate teaching as major factors affecting spoken English among Nigerians.
She explained that English remained a lingua franca for most Nigerians and that indigenous languages could influence the way people pronounced the words.
According to her, the quality of schools attended, the environment where people grow up and the people they interact with can also affect their diction.
“Mother tongue interference is one of the major factors. We are second-language users of English, so the languages we are used to tend to interfere when we speak,” she said.
The consultant explained that good diction involved more than speaking fluently, stressing the need for speakers to understand and correctly produce the sounds that make up English words.
She said that English had 44 speech sounds, comprising of 24 consonant and 20 vowel sounds.
Nimkur-Ikilama noted that some of the sounds could be difficult for Nigerian speakers because they were not found in some indigenous languages.
She demonstrated some of the difficult sounds and words during the training, guiding participants on their correct pronunciation.
The facilitator urged journalists on the need to pay attention to sounds rather than spelling alone.
She also advised journalists to practise speaking English regularly, read books, attend seminars, training programmes and listen to good speakers to improve their diction.
“English is a language, and the more you speak and use it, the more you learn. But when you keep quiet and do not speak, it tends to go away,” Nimkur-Ikilama said.
She also encouraged participants to make use of available learning resources, including the internet and artificial intelligence tools, have role models and mentors whose speeches they could study.
The principal consultant urged journalists to take diction seriously because their profession required them to communicate information clearly to a wide audience.
She also called on schools to strengthen diction, phonics and pronunciation lessons from the foundation level, as early exposure would help children develop better speech habits.
Nimkur-Ikilama advised parents to support their children by providing learning materials and expose them to environments where good English language was spoken.
She further expressed concern over the increasing use of pidgin among students, saying that children were often influenced by the speech patterns of their peers and immediate environment.
Giving his remarks, Mr Kevin Okunzuwa, the Head of Editorial Department, NAN, Lagos Operations, said that the workshop aimed at strengthening participants’ voice projection, public speaking and overall professional communication.
Okunzuwa, a Deputy Editor-in-Chief, said that the workshop, facilitated by Vethans Diction Consultancy, focused on diction and elocution.
He said that the training addressed common pronunciation challenges and introduced practical techniques to improve participants’ confidence in presentations, interviews, news delivery, voice-overs and other professional engagements.
Okunzuwa noted that the workshop focused on another step toward improving the organisation’s professional standards and communication skills.
He described the workshop as highly interactive, expressed participants’ enthusiasm and call for another session. ( NAN )( NAN )

items.title: Abure-led LP faction backs Tinubu for 2027

original_payload.original_title: Abure-led LP faction backs Tinubu for 2027
original_payload.original_body:
Politics  Abure-led LP faction backs Tinubu for 2027
By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   2 hours ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Perpetua Onuegbu
A faction of the Labour Party (LP), known as Labour Party (Legacy Members), has endorsed President Bola Tinubu for re-election in the 2027 general election.
The decision was contained in a communique issued after the faction’s National Executive Council (NEC) meeting on Monday in Abuja.
The meeting was attended by the factional National Chairman, Mr Julius Abure, members of the National Working Committee (NWC), state chairmen and secretaries, and other party stakeholders.
According to the communique, the NEC decided to support Tinubu after considering the candidates expected to contest the 2027 presidential election.
It said the faction intended to mobilise its supporters across the country in support of the President.
“After full evaluation of all the contesting candidates, NEC resolved to endorse President Bola Tinubu and campaign for him across the country for the 2027 general election,” the communique stated.
The group said it adopted the name Labour Party (Legacy Members) pending the outcome of an appeal at the Supreme Court challenging judgments of the Federal High Court and Court of Appeal, which recognised Sen. Nenadi Usman as leader of the party.
To mobilise support ahead of the election, the NEC approved a timetable for zonal town hall meetings across the country.
The meetings will begin in the South-West zone in Ogun on Nov. 28, followed by the South-East in Imo on Dec. 5 and the South-South in Akwa Ibom on Dec. 12.
Others are the North-Central in Nasarawa on Dec. 19, the North-East in Taraba on Jan. 2, 2027, and the North-West in Kaduna on Jan. 9, 2027.
The council directed state chairmen to extend the engagements to state, local government, ward and polling unit levels.
It also urged members to mobilise support for Tinubu ahead of the election.
The NEC also urged party members to promote peaceful political activities ahead of the 2027 general election.
Abure called on political leaders and their supporters to avoid actions that could lead to violence during the election period.
He urged parents to discourage their children from participating in violent protests and called on political leaders to promote peaceful political engagement.
(NAN)

items.title: Prix national de la simplification administrative : Les travaux d’évaluation des propositions lancés

original_payload.original_title: Prix national de la simplification administrative : Les travaux d’évaluation des propositions lancés
original_payload.original_body:
Le processus de sélection des meilleures propositions pour la simplification de l’administration publique béninoise franchit une nouvelle étape. Le lundi 23 novembre 2026, à Cotonou, le Ministre délégué auprès du Ministre de l’Économie et des Finances, chargé du Budget et de la Fonction publique, Monsieur Rodrigue CHAOU, a officiellement lancé les travaux d’évaluation des propositions pour l'attribution du Prix national de la simplification administrative. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence de Monsieur Mahuna AKPLOGAN, Ministre de la Transformation digitale et de l’Innovation, chargée de la stratégie nationale d’intelligence artificielle, et de Monsieur Nicolas YENOUSSI, Ministre délégué chargé des Finances et de la Microfinance.
Après la présentation de la grille d’évaluation et de la plateforme de notation la semaine dernière, les différentes commissions entrent désormais en fonction. Les travaux se dérouleront du 23 novembre au 4 décembre 2026, soit deux semaines consacrées à l’examen des propositions soumises.
Revenant sur les motivations de cette initiative présidentielle, le Ministre Rodrigue CHAOU a rappelé l'ambition du Gouvernement de rendre accessibles en ligne toutes les démarches administratives à l’horizon 2030. Il a souligné la volonté du Président de la République de construire la démarche de simplification administrative à partir des réalités vécues sur le terrain, notamment par les citoyens qui utilisent les services publics et les agents qui appliquent quotidiennement les procédures. Cette démarche participative a suscité plus de 5 000 propositions enregistrées dans les 14 secteurs concernés, entre le 29 octobre et le 12 novembre 2026.
Les commissions d’évaluation réunissent des compétences issues de l’administration publique, du secteur privé et de la société civile. À l’endroit des évaluateurs, le Ministre a insisté sur trois exigences fondamentales : l’honnêteté et l’impartialité, la rigueur dans l’analyse ainsi que la discrétion tout au long du processus. À l’issue de cette première phase, un jury national recevra les auteurs des meilleures propositions et procédera à la désignation des lauréats.
Outre la distinction des meilleures initiatives, toutes les propositions, primées ou non, viendront alimenter un vivier national de solutions. Les plus pertinentes feront l’objet d’une analyse approfondie, avant leur expérimentation avec les administrations concernées. Une démarche qui entend faire de l’expérience des usagers et de l’innovation collective des leviers concrets de modernisation et d’amélioration du service public béninois.

items.title: Salon national du livre : La poésie en apothéose pour clôturer l’édition 2026

original_payload.original_title: Salon national du livre : La poésie en apothéose pour clôturer l’édition 2026
original_payload.original_body:
La cérémonie de clôture de la 5 ème  édition du Salon national du livre a eu ce dimanche 22 novembre au Palais des congrès de Cotonou. C’est également l’occasion des poètes d’ici et d’ailleurs de vivre sur scène la grande nuit de la poésie.
Des proses poétiques entonnées, des vers en hémistiches récités et des déclamations scéniques exécutées. C’est ce qui a alimenté la grande nuit de la poésie ayant marqué la clôture du Salon national du livre, édition 2026. Des voix, alliant poème et slam se sont élevées sur scène pour transmettre le plaisir d’écouter. Plusieurs acteurs venus du Burkina Fasso, du Congo, de Haïti, du Togo et du Bénin ont émerveillé le public.
Pour Florent Couao-Zotti, délégué général du Salon National du Livre, avoir cette touche finale du spectacle qu’est la grande nuit de la poésie, donne l’assurance que la poésie est vivante, dynamique et rassemble. « Et c’est pour cela que nous avons articulé le thème ainsi : ‘’La poésie dans tous ses états’’. Depuis jeudi, mon équipe et moi avions pris la mesure de l’engouement que le Salon du Livre a suscité, surtout au niveau de cette édition où collèges, établissements scolaires et universités se sont joints à cette célébration pour dire haut et fort que le livre reste et restera toujours un compagnon. On dit très souvent qu’un peuple qui ne lit pas est un peuple inculte, un peuple qui ne lit pas est un peuple sans instruction. Et je suis persuadé qu’avec les efforts que nous faisons tous les jours, à travers diverses initiatives, nos peuples deviendront beaucoup plus forts parce qu’il y a justement la littérature, la poésie et tous les genres littéraires qui consacrent l’humanité dans ses différentes complexités », a-t-il fait remarquer.
Il n’a pas manqué d’adresser ses remerciements au ministre de tutelle. « Je voudrais remercier tout d’abord mon ministre de la culture, des arts et du patrimoine qui n’a ménagé aucun effort pour que cette édition se tienne. Vous l’avez vécu en direct, de manière totale, les écrivains que nous avons invités de partout, de Pointe-Noire, de Libreville, et qui sont venus avec leur arme à la main, c’est-à-dire leur poésie. Nous sommes heureux d’avoir partagé ces quelques moments avec vous et je voudrais ici remercier la coordination de cet événement », a salué Florent Couao-Zotti. Les invités et le public se disent heureux aussi d’avoir partagé ce moment merveilleux de la littérature qui met en lumière la poésie. Les regards sont désormais tournés vers l’édition prochaine.

items.title: Géographie d’un corps déplacé : Une première restitution fait sensation à l’EITB

original_payload.original_title: Géographie d’un corps déplacé : Une première restitution fait sensation à l’EITB
original_payload.original_body:
Un spectacle de restitution a eu lieu ce dimanche 22 novembre à l’Ecole Internationale du Théâtre du Bénin à Cotonou. C’est l’occasion pour les acteurs retenus dans le cadre du projet « Géographie d’un corps déplacé » d’émerveiller le public avec ce qu’ils ont appris pendant ces deux dernières semaines. Ce projet est une initiative de Cybelline de Souza, artiste pluridisciplinaire, comédienne, metteuse en scène et danseuse.
Les mouvements flexibles du corps transmettent de l’émotion et véhiculent des messages. C’est dans cette ambiance de spectacle que les 15 candidats retenus dans le cadre du projet « Géographie d’un corps déplacé » ont plongé le public dont les acclamations ont témoigné de la de joie et de la satisfaction.
Les différents tableaux artistiques que présentent les incubés sont le résultat de ce qu’ils ont acquis durant deux semaines. Ce rendez-vous de restitution a aussi permis aux formateurs d’évaluer les acquis des incubés et au public de découvrir le travail en cours et l’émergence des futurs talents du théâtre physique au Bénin.
Cette première étape du parcours, prévu pour durer 11 mois, a pris en compte deux premiers modules à savoir : Dramaturgie du corps dans l’espace théâtral dispensé par Cybelline de-Souza ; Musique, rythme et improvisation dans l’espace théâtral assuré par Samuel Messerli. Cybelline de-Souza a fait part des raisons qui l’ont poussée à initier le projet. « C’est mon envie de partager ce que j’ai appris en Suisse à l’Accademia Dimitri, Haute école spécialisée dans le théâtre physique. J’ai fait un Master en Théâtre physique, Théâtre du corps, où j’ai appris à utiliser mon corps après mon passage ici à l’EITB. Je me suis dit que tout le monde n’a pas l’opportunité de partir. Moi j’ai eu la chance de partir et j’ai appris. Donc, je me suis dit que c’était important de revenir et de transmettre », a-t-elle signalé.
Samuel Messerli se dit satisfait du résultat. « On est contents de voir déjà le premier résultat et surtout on se réjouit du résultat final », s’est-il réjoui. Les candidats retenus n’ont pas regretté d’avoir fait partie de l’aventure.
« Je suis très contente parce que le corps, c’est quelque chose que je souhaitais explorer depuis. J’aime explorer l’espace, le langage corporel dans l’espace. C’était une occasion à ne pas rater et que j’ai saisie quand Cybelline de-Souza a lancé l’appel à candidature pour ce projet. Et je suis très contente, zéro regret d’avoir participé à cet atelier, à cette formation. Je suis très contente et j’espère que ce premier pas va donner suite à d’autres étapes », a indiqué Carole, étudiante à l’EITB.
Alougbine Dine, fondateur de l’EITB, est également satisfait du résultat et a salué l’initiative. « Avec ce que j’ai vu ce soir, je retiens tout simplement qu’il n’y a pas de frontière entre le théâtre et la danse. Tous deux sont des arts de mouvement. La preuve est là », a-t-il déclaré.
Un autre rendez-vous de restitution est pris pour le 12 décembre prochain à L’EITB après deux autres modules de formation qui seront assurés par Carole Lokossou et Carlos Zinsou. A noter le projet est porté par Théâtre au Compteur, avec le soutien de la Coopération suisse au Bénin. L’initiatrice n’a pas manqué de remercier l’EITB, l’Institut français du Bénin et d’autres partenaires pour leur soutien dans la mise en œuvre du projet

items.title: W. Darfur IDPs decry appalling living conditions

original_payload.original_title: W. Darfur IDPs decry appalling living conditions
original_payload.original_body:
Displaced women sheltering in accommodation centers across Sudan’s West Darfur State have lamented deteriorating living conditions and dwindling humanitarian assistance amid soaring prices of essential commodities and poor agricultural yields due to poor rainfall.
They appealed to humanitarian organizations to intervene urgently and provide food and essential healthcare supplies.
A woman who spoke to Radio Tamazuj on condition of anonymity said displaced families are enduring increasingly harsh conditions because of the limited assistance provided by humanitarian organizations.
“This year’s agricultural season has been disappointing due to inadequate rainfall, which has adversely affected crop production, compounding the hardship caused by the sharp rise in the prices of basic commodities,” she lamented.
Another displaced woman described the conditions as extremely difficult, stressing that they were in desperate need of humanitarian assistance to meet their basic needs.
Meanwhile, Daw Al-Bait Adam Yagoub, Director of the Sudanese Agency for Relief and Humanitarian Operations in West Darfur State, revealed that assistance provided by international organizations operating in the state this year had not exceeded 5 percent.
“The shortfall is because of challenges associated with shrinking humanitarian funding budgets and shortages of food, medicines and other relief supplies,” he stated. “The World Food Programme (WFP) announced reductions in the assistance it provides in El Geneina and Kereinik.”
According to Al-Bait, more than 60,000 families had arrived in West Darfur from other parts of Sudan.
He explained that El Geneina alone was hosting between 25,000 and 30,000 families across more than 18 displacement shelters. He stressed that these facilities had received no humanitarian assistance over the past seven months.
Yagoub further disclosed that meetings had been held with international organizations and United Nations agencies to strengthen the humanitarian response and increase assistance to affected populations in the coming year.

items.title: South Sudan urged to strengthen petroleum governance before courting investors

original_payload.original_title: South Sudan urged to strengthen petroleum governance before courting investors
original_payload.original_body:
Policy and political analyst Boboya James Edmond has called on the Government of South Sudan to prioritize institutional reforms, transparency, accountability, and regulatory enforcement before expanding foreign investment in the country’s petroleum sector.
Edmond, who serves as Chief Executive Officer of the Institute of Social Policy and Research (ISPR) in South Sudan, made the remarks in response to a recent statement by Caretaker Minister of Petroleum Awow Daniel Chuang affirming the government’s readiness to welcome foreign investors and establish new partnerships in the oil industry.
Edmond stressed that attracting foreign capital must go hand in hand with deep institutional reforms.
“It is a timely opportunity for South Sudan to rethink its petroleum governance and investment policy framework,” he said. “Attracting foreign investors must be accompanied by institutional reforms, policy coherence, and accountability mechanisms to ensure that petroleum resources generate broad-based and sustainable development benefits.”
He outlined several priority areas that the government and the Ministry of Petroleum must address to ensure foreign investments deliver lasting national development.
There must be strengthening of the legal and regulatory framework governing the petroleum sector to ensure policy consistency and predictable investment conditions,” Edmond said. “This includes transparent licensing procedures, clear contractual obligations, and the effective enforcement of existing petroleum laws.”
He emphasized the need for strict transparency in negotiating foreign investment agreements, production-sharing arrangements, and revenue management mechanisms. Strengthening oversight institutions and public disclosure requirements, he argued, would minimize corruption risks, build public confidence, and safeguard national interests.
“Foreign investment agreements must incorporate binding provisions for technology transfer, professional training, and knowledge sharing to progressively build national technical capacity and reduce long-term dependence on foreign experts,” Edmond counseled. “Petroleum expansion must be accompanied by mandatory Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs), strict pollution control measures, remediation obligations, and genuine community consultations. Protecting livelihoods, ecosystems, and public health must be central to investment decision-making.”
He added that seamless coordination among petroleum, finance, environmental, labor, and trade institutions is essential for policy coherence.
Edmond called for sound revenue management that accounts for intergenerational equity, ensuring oil wealth benefits both present and future generations. He urged the government to leverage foreign partnerships to stimulate diversification into agriculture, agro-processing, energy, infrastructure, and manufacturing.
“Petroleum resources should serve as a catalyst for economic transformation rather than reinforce the country’s structural dependence on oil exports,” he said.
On the importance of equitable benefit-sharing for oil-producing communities, Edmond also called on the government to establish credible institutional mechanisms for engaging investors, resolving disputes, and aligning commitments with national priorities such as South Sudan’s Vision 2040.
He contends that success must be judged by the quality of investments, the strength of governance institutions, the protection of national interests, and tangible development outcomes for citizens.
“The fundamental policy challenge is to move from an extractive petroleum investment model toward a responsible, transparent, and development-oriented petroleum governance framework,” Edmond said, adding that foreign investment must serve the national economy and the well-being of South Sudanese citizens rather than simply expand oil production.
On Wednesday last week, the Caretaker Minister of Petroleum Awow Daniel Chuang outlined the Ministry of Petroleum’s strategy to leverage the nation’s vast hydrocarbon reserves to drive sustainable economic growth and create employment opportunities for South Sudanese youth.
“South Sudan holds enormous hydrocarbon resources, with approximately 90 percent of our reserves still underdeveloped and less than 15 percent of the area explored,” he said at the time. “This presents a significant investment opportunity across the entire petroleum value chain.”

items.title: SSPDF commander blames Governor Lobong for deploying army, Nakeke killings

original_payload.original_title: SSPDF commander blames Governor Lobong for deploying army, Nakeke killings
original_payload.original_body:
The commander of the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF) Seventh Infantry Division in Eastern Equatoria State has denied allegations linking him to a deadly incident in Nakeke, Kapoeta, accusing Governor Louis Lobong Lojore of deploying security forces to the area without consulting him.
Maj. Gen. Okot David Awai said the deployment occurred while he was away from the division headquarters and that he was neither consulted nor informed before troops were sent to the gold-mining area.
Speaking to Radio Tamazuj on Monday during an exclusive interview, Gen. Okot said he later travelled to the area and found no rebel activity, contrary to claims he said had been reported to the military headquarters.
“When I reached there, there was no rebel activity,” he stated. “I came to find that it was only just a misunderstanding; a dispute between him (Lobong) and the youths of the area.”
According to the commander, the dispute involved local youths demanding what they considered their rightful share of gold extracted by a mining company operating in the area.
He alleged that the deployment of security forces was intended to push the youths and the surrounding communities away from the mining site rather than address their grievances.
Gen. Okot said the incident resulted in loss of life and property, but he did not provide details of the casualties or the extent of the damage.
He challenged Governor Lobong to publicly explain the circumstances that led to the deployment, saying the governor should account for the decision because it was made without his consultation.
The commander also rejected allegations circulating on social media linking him to the incident, saying he has been waiting for the governor to explain what happened. He said nearly 24 days had passed since the incident, but the governor had remained silent, prompting him to issue a public clarification.
“That is why we come forward to clear the air and to tell the public that the office of the commander is innocent regarding what has happened in Nakeke,” Gen. Okot stated.
His remarks offer a different account of the incident, presenting it as a dispute over access to gold-mining proceeds rather than a security operation against armed opposition forces.
He accused unnamed politicians of exploiting security institutions to advance personal interests and warned against using the army to settle disagreements between civilians and those involved in resource extraction.
“I will not allow any politician to use our army for their selfish interests. The army is there to protect everybody,” Gen. Okot said.
The commander maintained that the SSPDF’s responsibility is to protect civilians, their property, and the country’s territorial integrity, arguing that disputes involving civilians should primarily be handled by the police and local authorities.
He said state and county officials should pursue dialogue to resolve community grievances instead of treating residents who raise concerns as rebels.
“Pursue dialogue rather than labelling your own community as rebels because of your greedy, selfish interests to gain what you want from them, which is not good,” Gen. Okot admonished.
The senior officer also appealed to residents not to take the law into their hands, warning that violence could expose innocent civilians to more suffering.
He urged communities to use peaceful dialogue to address disagreements, particularly those involving natural resources, and cautioned politicians against exploiting local grievances.
The commander further accused some political actors of failing to deliver services while seeking to control community resources, saying such practices risk worsening tensions between residents and authorities.
Gen. Okot reiterated that the army should not be drawn into civilian disputes and that security forces should operate within their legal mandate.
The efforts to reach the governor’s office for comment were futile.

items.title: Analyst: Resources, supply lines reshape Sudan’s balance of war

original_payload.original_title: Analyst: Resources, supply lines reshape Sudan’s balance of war
original_payload.original_body:
A Sudanese military analyst and retired Air Force Lieutenant, Al-Tayyib Malkabi, believes that the rapidly evolving military developments in Sudan’s Blue Nile Region and Kordofan reflect a shift in combat operations.
He told Radio Tamazuj that control over vital resources, supply lines and strategic locations is assuming increasing significance as hostilities expand and as the warring parties seek to extend their territorial influence.
His assessment comes in the wake of a marked military escalation in the Blue Nile Region in recent weeks, with fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), allied with forces operating under the Tasis Alliance, spreading to several areas along the Kurmuk and Geissan fronts, accompanied by shifts in control over strategically significant positions.
In the latest developments, the RSF and the Sudan Founding Alliance, known as Tasis, announced on 20 November that they had captured the administrative headquarters of Bau Locality and Village 12 along the Geissan front. Meanwhile, the command of the SAF Fourth Infantry Division confirmed that it had repelled an attack on the Dering area along the Kurmuk front.
Village 12 lies approximately 40 kilometers from Damazin, while Bau and Dering constitute forward positions along the Kurmuk axis leading towards the regional capital.
These developments were preceded by an announcement by Tasis forces in early November that they had seized control of the Sali area. The area holds strategic significance owing to its location along the road connecting Kurmuk and Damazin, as well as its proximity to mining areas, giving control over it military and economic dimensions that extend beyond its immediate geographical importance.
In his assessment of these developments, Lt. Col. Malkabi draws a connection between the shifting battlefield dynamics and stalled political efforts.
“The lack of progress in diplomatic initiatives pursued through the Quad and Quintet frameworks has contributed to the persistent political deadlock, while the warring parties have increasingly sought to consolidate their military positions and strengthen their leverage on the ground,” he stated.
These developments have raised concerns over the potential expansion of hostilities around Damazin, the region’s administrative and military center of gravity, amid mounting displacement and deteriorating humanitarian conditions in conflict-affected areas.
Lt. Col. Malkabi contends that Sudan’s military operational landscape is increasingly shaped by the strategic interplay between resources and supply lines.
“Control over towns and areas of geographical significance is no longer, in itself, the sole benchmark of military progress.” The analyst argues. “Rather, the strategic value of a particular location is increasingly determined by the logistical and economic opportunities it affords, as well as the capacity it gives the controlling party to manoeuvre, secure supply lines or disrupt them.”
This dynamic is particularly evident in the Blue Nile and Kordofan regions, where control over roads, corridors and economically productive areas has become intertwined with military calculations.
Consequently, certain locations have acquired strategic significance disproportionate to their population size or administrative standing, owing to their role in connecting military deployment areas and operational centers.

items.title: Sennar state resumes banana exports to Saudi Arabia

original_payload.original_title: Sennar state resumes banana exports to Saudi Arabia
original_payload.original_body:
Sudan’s Sennar state has exported its first shipment of bananas to Saudi Arabia since the war began in April 2023, a state official said on Monday, following an earlier consignment to Jordan.
Nour al-Din Dawoud Musa, director-general of Sennar’s Ministry of Production and Economic Resources, said the shipment was prepared at the Sudanese Centre for Horticultural Export Treatment in the Sabounabi area.
He described the shipment as a sign of renewed activity in the state’s horticultural sector, which has been disrupted by the conflict.
The official did not disclose the shipment’s volume or value.
Musa said the ministry would support efforts to increase production and improve product quality to meet international export standards.
Awad Mohammed Dawoud, the state’s agricultural quarantine director, said the shipment had completed the required phytosanitary procedures before export.
He said the centre handles the sorting, grading, packaging and treatment of bananas destined for export.
Abdelrahman Mohammed Abdelmajid, secretary-general of the National Chamber of Fruit and Vegetable Exporters, outlined the export preparation process, from receiving and sorting the bananas to packaging and loading them into refrigerated trucks.
Sennar’s agricultural sector has suffered significant disruption during the war, including damage to infrastructure and shortages of production inputs. The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces controlled parts of the state before the Sudanese army recaptured Sinja, the state capital, on Nov. 23, 2024.
The army announced on March 5, 2025, that it had regained control of the entire state, including the towns of al-Mazmum and al-Dali.

items.title: Ter Manyang leaves rights activism for academia

original_payload.original_title: Ter Manyang leaves rights activism for academia
original_payload.original_body:
A renowned South Sudanese human rights activist, Ter Manyang Gatwech, on Monday announced plans to transition from frontline civil society activism to academia after 13 years of advocating for human rights, peacebuilding and social justice in the country.
Manyang, the Executive Director of the Nile Institute for Human Rights Studies (NIHRS), told Radio Tamazuj that he had decided to pursue a new professional direction following the completion of a Master of Arts in Transformational Leadership, specializing in Gender Studies and Women’s Rights, at the University of Juba.
He graduated on 21 November 2026, but said he was unable to attend the ceremony in person due to “security concerns.”
Reflecting on his journey since 2013, Manyang said his work in human rights advocacy had involved significant personal and professional challenges, including security threats and risks associated with speaking out against human rights violations and demanding accountability.
“I feel that I have spent many years in civil society work, particularly in human rights advocacy, since 2013,” he said. “It has been a challenging journey, with numerous risks and sacrifices.”
He said his academic achievement had prompted him to reconsider how best to contribute to social transformation, adding that academia would provide an opportunity to engage more deeply with societal challenges.
“Following my academic achievement, I have decided to transition from frontline civil society activism to academia,” he stated. “I believe this transition will provide me with an opportunity to deepen my understanding of society and the world through academic research, teaching, knowledge production, and intellectual engagement.”
Manyang’s work over the past 13 years has focused on human rights advocacy, peacebuilding, transitional justice, gender equality, and the promotion of fundamental freedoms in South Sudan.
However, he said the move to academia should not be misconstrued as abandonment of those causes, but rather as a shift in the approach through which he intends to pursue them.
He said research, education, and evidence-based policy engagement could provide additional avenues for addressing social and governance challenges while complementing the work of civil society organizations.
Meanwhile, the Nile Institute for Human Rights Studies is expected to continue operating as an independent research institution, with a renewed focus on research, capacity building and advocacy.
According to Manyang, the institute will prioritize evidence-based research, policy analysis, documentation and publications covering human rights, transitional justice, gender equality, governance, democracy and peacebuilding.
It also plans to provide professional training, workshops, seminars and educational programmes for civil society organizations, human rights defenders, government institutions and other stakeholders.
On advocacy, the institute intends to use research findings to promote policy dialogue, engage relevant stakeholders and make recommendations aimed at strengthening human rights protection and democratic governance.
Manyang expressed appreciation to fellow human rights defenders, civil society colleagues, development partners, academic institutions and individuals who supported him throughout his years of advocacy.
The Nile Institute for Human Rights Studies is an independent research institution working to promote human rights, justice, gender equality, peacebuilding and democratic governance through research, capacity building and evidence-based advocacy.

items.title: Dakar experience inspires South Sudanese youth to demand opportunities at home

original_payload.original_title: Dakar experience inspires South Sudanese youth to demand opportunities at home
original_payload.original_body:
For 24-year-old Deng Wiyual Nyang, travelling to Dakar for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games was an eye-opening experience that left him questioning why young South Sudanese continue to risk their lives crossing the Mediterranean Sea in search of better opportunities when their own country has abundant natural resources.
After witnessing the development and opportunities available to young people in Senegal, Deng returned with a dream of seeing similar progress at home and calling on the government to invest more in young people and give them opportunities to shape the country’s future.
Speaking to Radio Tamazuj on Monday in Juba, Deng, a member of the Youth Protection Team working with the Nonviolent Peace Force (NP), said the six-day visit to Senegal exposed him to developments and opportunities that he hopes can be replicated in South Sudan.
“When I came back after those six days that we spent in Senegal, I feel like if I have any ability or any position in my country, I could make a lot of developments,” he said. “Where we went, we got good developments, a lot of things.”
According to Deng, among other developed institutions he witnessed in Dakar are sports complexes such as stadia and good tourism sites.
He said the experience strengthened his belief that young people can contribute to national development if given opportunities and meaningful participation in decision-making.
Deng expressed concern over the increasing number of South Sudanese youths leaving the country for Europe through dangerous migration routes, particularly across Libya and the Mediterranean Sea.
He said many young people are driven to leave because of unemployment and limited opportunities despite the country’s abundant natural resources.
“They are putting their life at risk so that they will go and look for a better life. And that is not because we do not have good companies or resources. We have more resources, but the opportunities have not been given to the youth to work for themselves,” he said. “The government should create more opportunities for young people to work and contribute to the country’s development rather than forcing them to seek a future abroad.”
“Also, we need young people to participate in parliament to raise our voice so that our rights are respected,” Deng said.
Beyond employment and political participation, he said his experience in Senegal taught him the importance of peace and peaceful coexistence.
DENG currently works with Youth Protection Teams, community structures supported by the Nonviolent Peace Force to identify challenges faced by young people and report them to community and government leaders. He said the teams also engage unemployed and vulnerable young people, including those who have lost hope of continuing their education, through community activities and online platforms.
Just like Deng, Nyanuer Wiyual Manytap, another member of the team, said they are excited about the opportunity to participate in the programme and promote peace through sports and development.
Meanwhile, Moses Moi Kenyi, the Partnership Manager at Nonviolent Peace Force and head of the delegation to Senegal, said the trip was intended to expose South Sudanese youth to international experiences and encourage them to become active contributors to peacebuilding.
He said the delegation comprised four young people and himself, with participants selected from Youth Protection Teams and the South Sudan National Olympics Committee, mainly from the Upper Nile region.
Kenyi said the French Embassy supported the trip, which was part of efforts to empower young people to see themselves as agents of change rather than victims of conflict.
“They are not taking themselves as victims of conflict, but they are solutions to the issues that are happening in South Sudan, especially conflict,” he said.
He added that the visit also aimed to prepare young people to engage their communities in peacebuilding activities and contribute to development initiatives planned along the Nile Corridor, particularly in fishing and agriculture.
“South Sudan has the ability; we cannot be asking for food when we have the Nile,” Kenyi said.
He called on national and international leaders to invest more in peacebuilding, arguing that addressing the root causes of conflict would reduce the country’s dependence on humanitarian assistance.
Kenyi said the young people returned to South Sudan on Friday after attending the closing ceremony of the Youth Olympic Games and interacting with participants and partner organizations from other countries.
He expressed hope that the experience would encourage the delegation to share lessons from Senegal with other young people and promote peace and development in their communities.
The five-member delegation, drawn mainly from the Upper Nile region, travelled to Senegal late last month to attend the Dakar 2026 Olympic Games that started on the 31 st  October and concluded on the 13 th  of this month. The visit was facilitated by the Nonviolent Peace Force, with financial support from the French Embassy in Juba.

original_payload.original_title: Madagascar : Des mandats d’arrêt requis contre Andry Rajoelina et son ancien Premier ministre
original_payload.original_body:
Madagascar : Des mandats d’arrêt requis contre Andry Rajoelina et son ancien Premier ministre
admin
novembre 24, 2026
1 minutes de lecture
126 vues
L’ancien président malgache Andry Rajoelina fait l’objet d’une demande de mandat d’arrêt dans le cadre de l’affaire des Boeing 777 envoyés en Iran. Le parquet anticorruption a également requis un mandat d’arrêt contre son ancien Premier ministre, Christian Ntsay. Selon les médias malgaches, ces réquisitions ont été annoncées samedi.
L’affaire concerne cinq Boeing 777 immatriculés à Madagascar et intégrés, en juillet 2025, à la flotte d’une compagnie aérienne iranienne, alors que l’Iran fait l’objet de sanctions internationales.
Andry Rajoelina et Christian Ntsay, qui ont quitté Madagascar en octobre 2025, sont notamment soupçonnés de faits liés au financement du terrorisme. Les deux anciens dirigeants sont concernés par cette procédure judiciaire.

items.title: Tchad : L’Assemblée nationale adopte le projet de budget de l’État pour l’exercice 2027

original_payload.original_title: Tchad : L’Assemblée nationale adopte le projet de budget de l’État pour l’exercice 2027
original_payload.original_body:
Les députés ont adopté, lundi 23 novembre 2026, en séance plénière au Palais de la Démocratie, le projet de loi de finances portant budget général de l’État pour l’exercice 2027. Ce budget prévoit des ressources de 3 070 milliards de FCFA et des dépenses de 3 007 milliards de FCFA, soit un excédent prévisionnel de 63 milliards de FCFA, dons compris.
Réunis en séance plénière au Palais de la Démocratie, les députés ont procédé à l’examen et au vote du projet de loi de finances pour l’exercice budgétaire 2027. La séance était présidée par  Ali Kolotou Tchaïmi , président de l’Assemblée nationale.
À cette occasion, le projet de budget a été présenté aux élus par  Tahir Hamid Nguilin , Ministre d’État, Ministre des Finances, du Budget, de l’Économie, du Plan et de la Coopération internationale. La ministre, Secrétaire générale du Gouvernement,  Dr Ramatou Mahamat Houtouin , ainsi que plusieurs autres membres du Gouvernement ont également pris part à cette séance parlementaire.
Sur le plan financier, le budget de l’État pour l’année 2027 est arrêté à 3 070 milliards de FCFA en ressources, enregistrant une hausse de 35 % par rapport à l’exercice précédent. Les dépenses, quant à elles, sont estimées à 3 007 milliards de FCFA, soit une progression de 19 %.
Cette configuration budgétaire fait ressortir un solde excédentaire prévisionnel de 63 milliards de FCFA, y compris les dons. Ces projections traduisent les grandes orientations financières retenues par le Gouvernement pour la gestion des finances publiques au cours de l’année 2027.
Au terme des échanges et des débats entre les députés, le projet de loi de finances a été adopté. Ce texte entend notamment soutenir la croissance économique, renforcer la mobilisation des ressources internes, moderniser le système fiscal et accompagner le processus de décentralisation.
Avec l’adoption de ce budget, le Gouvernement dispose ainsi d’un nouveau cadre financier pour mettre en œuvre ses priorités économiques et sociales au titre de l’exercice 2027.

items.title: Why S Korea issued air raid alert after Russian jets flew near its airspace

original_payload.original_title: Why S Korea issued air raid alert after Russian jets flew near its airspace
original_payload.original_body:
South Korea has scrambled fighter jets and issued brief air raid warnings for residents of an island after Russian military planes approached its airspace over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan.
Russian jets on Tuesday briefly entered South Korea’s air defence identification zone (ADIZ), an aerial buffer area between countries, South Korea’s military said, adding that “multiple” Russian aircraft were “on the verge” of entering the country’s ⁠airspace over Ulleung Island.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth
list 2 of 3  Russia warns Ukraine of ‘dangerous trend’ after Libya and Baltic attacks
list 3 of 3  EU plans sports ban in sweeping new Russia sanctions proposal
end of list
“Airspace intrusion was anticipated. Therefore, to protect the safety of our people, we issued a warning pre-emptively,” Jang Do-young, a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said.
Authorities had earlier issued an alert that a North Korean plane had made an incursion, which would have been a significant escalation in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war after the 1950-1953 Korean War ended with an armistice and not a peace treaty. South Korea later issued a correction saying no North Korean jet was involved.
Here’s everything we know about the incident:
Why did South Korea tell residents to take shelter?
According to the Joint Chiefs of Staff, about five Russian military aircraft entered South Korea’s ADIZ on Tuesday morning. There was no intrusion of South Korea’s airspace by the Russian aircraft in the end, the South Korean military said.
Jang said the aircraft came “very close” to the airspace above Ulleung Island, which is home to 9,000 people and lies 120km (75 miles) off the northeastern coast of South Korea. South Korean fighter jets conducted “tactical manoeuvres” to prevent any incident, the Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

items.title: Russian attack kills two people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia

original_payload.original_title: Russian attack kills two people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia
original_payload.original_body:
A Russian air attack on Zaporizhzhia in Ukraine has killed two people and wounded more than 40, including an infant, the day after Kyiv said its drones sank a Russian warship in a Libyan port far from the front lines of the war.
Russia’s dawn raid on the city in southeast Ukraine destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, regional officials said on Tuesday.

It came as the two warring sides continued long-range attacks, launching hundreds of drones overnight.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said air defences intercepted and destroyed 699 Ukrainian drones over seven regions, occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 355 drones flew towards the capital overnight and 63 were shot down as they approached.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Amin Dorghami said it had been a “long time” since Moscow had been targeted with as many drones.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 96 drones overnight, with hits at 13 locations and 73 shot down or jammed.
